sp.speaker: Arsenio
sp.ab: LEandro paid all.

sp.speaker: Mil
sp.ab:
’Tis his usuall custome,
And requisite he should: he has now put off
The Funerall black, (your rich heirs weares with joy,
When he pretends to weep for his dead Father,)
Your gathering Sires, so long heape muck together,
That their kind Sonnes, to rid them of their care
Wish them in heaven; Or if they take a taste
Of Purgatory by the way, it matters not:
Provided they remove hence; What is befalne
To his Father, in the other world, I ask not,
I am sure his prayre is heard: would I could use one
For mine, in the same method.

sp.speaker: Arsen
sp.ab:
Fy upon thee.
This is prophane,

sp.speaker: Mil
sp.ab:
Good Doctor, doe not schoole me,
For a fault you are not free from: On my life
Were all Heires in Cordoba, put too their oathes
They would confes se with me, ’tis a sound Tenet:
I am sure Leonardo do’s.

sp.speaker: Ars
sp.ab:
He is th’ owner
Of a faire Estate.

sp.speaker: Mil
sp.ab:
And fairly he deserves it,
He’s a royall Fellow: yet observes a meane
In all his courses, carefull to on whom
He showres his bounties: he that’s liberall
To all alike, may doe a Good by chance,
But never out of Judgement: This invites
The prime men of the Citie to frequent
All places he resorts to, and are happy
In his sweet Converse.

sp.speaker: Ars
sp.ab:
Don Jaime the Brother
To the Grandee Don Henrique, appeares much taken
With his behaviour.

sp.speaker: Mil
sp.ab:
There is something more in’t:
H[e] needs his Purse, and knowes how to make use on’t,
[’Tis n]ow in fashion your Don, that’s poore,
To vow all Leagues of friendship with a Merchant
That can supply his wants, and howsoe’re
Don Jaime’s noble borne, his elder Brother
Don Henrique rich, and his Revenues long since
Encreasing by marrying with a wealthy Heire
Call’d Madam Violante, he yet holdsJamy Leandro & Ascanio be ready
A hard hand o’er Jaime, allowing him
A bare annuity onely.

sp.speaker: Ars
sp.ab:
Yet ’tis said
He hath no child, and by the Lawes of Spaine
If he die without is sue, Don Jaime
Inherits his Estate.

sp.speaker: Mil
sp.ab:
Why that’s the reason
Of their so many jarres: Though the young Lord
Be sick of the elder Brother, and in reason
Should flatter, and observe him, he’s of a nature
Too bold, and fierce, to stoop so, but beares up,
Presuming on his hopes.

sp.speaker: Ars
sp.ab:
What’s the young Lad
That all of em makes so much of?

sp.speaker: Mil
sp.ab:
’Tis a sweet-One,
And the best condition’d youth, I ever saw yet,
So humble and so affable, that he wins
The love of all that know him, and so modest,
That (in despight of povertie) he would starve
Rather then aske a courtesie; He’s the Sonne
Of a poore cast-Captaine, one Octavio,
And She, that once was calld th’ faire Iacinta,
Is happy in being his Mother: for his sake.

(Though in their Fortunes falne) they are esteem’d of,
And cherish’d by the best. O here they come,
I now may spare his Character, but observe him,
Hee’l justifie my report.

sp.speaker: Ia
sp.ab:
My good Ascanio
Repaire more often to me: above Women
Thou ever shalt be welcome.

sp.speaker: Asc
sp.ab:
My Lord your favours
May quickly teach a raw untutour’d Youth
To be both rude and sawcie.

sp.speaker: Leandro
sp.ab:
You cannot be
Too frequent, where you are so desir’d:
And give me leave (dear friend) to be your Rivall
In part of his Affection: I will buy it
At any rate.

sp.speaker: Ia
sp.ab:
Stood I but now pos sess’d Of
28
Of what my future hope presages to me,
I then would make it cleare thou hadst a Patron
That would not say but do: yet as I am,
Be mine, I’le not receive thee as a servant,
But as my Son (and though I want my self)
No Page attending in the Court of Spain
Shall find a kinder master.

sp.speaker: Ars
sp.ab:
I beseech you
That my refusall of so great an offer
May make no ill construction, ’tis not pride
(That common vice is farre from my condition)
That makes you a denyall to receive
A favour I should sue for: nor the fashion
Which the country followes, in which to be a servant
In those that groan beneath the heavy weight
Of povertie is held an argument
Of a base and abject mind, I wish my yeares
Were fit to do you a service in a nature
That might become a Gentleman (give me leave
To think my self one) My father serv’d the King
As a Captain in the field; and though his fortune
Return’d him home a poore man, he was rich
In reputation, and wounds fairly taken.
Nor am I by his ill succes se deterr’d,
I rather feel a strong desire that swayes me
To follow his Profes sion, and if heaven
Hath marked me out to be a man, how proud,
In the service of my Country, should I be,
To traile a pike under your brave command.
There, I would follow you as a guid to honour,
Though all the horrours of the Warre made up
To stop my passage.

sp.speaker: Ia
sp.ab:
Thou art a hopefull Boye,
And it was bravely spoken: For this answer,
I love thee more then ever.

sp.speaker: Mil
sp.ab:
Pitty such seedsHenrique be ready
Of promising courage should not grow and prosper

sp.speaker: Ang
sp.ab:
What ever his reputed Parents bee,
He hath a mind that speakes him right and noble.

sp.speaker: Lea
sp.ab:
You make him blush: it needs not sweet Ascanio,
We may heare praises when they are deserv’d,
Or modestie unwounded. By my life
I would adde something to the building up
So faire a mind, and if till you are fit
To beare Armes in the field, you’l spend some yeares
In Salamanca, I’le supply your studies
With all conveniences.

sp.speaker: Ars
sp.ab:
Your goodnes se (Signiors)
And charitable favours overwhelm me.
If I were of your blood, you could not be
More tender of me: what then can I pay
(A poore boy and a stranger) but a heart
Bound to your service? with what willingnes
I would receive (good Sir) your noble offer,
Heaven can beare witnes for me: but alas
Should I embrace the meanes to raise my fortunes,
I must destroy the lives of my poore Parents
(To whom I ow my being) they in me
Place all their comforts, and (as if I were
The light of their dim eyes) are so indulgent
They cannot brook one short dayes absence from me;
And (what will hardly win belief) though young,
I am their steward and their nurse: the bounties
VVhich others bestow on me serves to sustain ’em,
And to forsake them in their age, in me
VVere more then murther.

sp.speaker: Ang
sp.ab:
This is a kind of begging
VVould make a Broker charitable.

sp.speaker: Mil
sp.ab:
Here (sweet heart)
I wish that it were more.

sp.speaker: Lean
sp.ab:
VVhen this is spent,
Seek for supply from me

sp.speaker: Ja
sp.ab:
Thy pietie
For ever be remembered: nay take all,
Though ’t were my exhibition to a Royall☨
For one whole yeare.

sp.speaker: Asc
sp.ab: High heavens reward your goodnes.

sp.speaker: Hen
sp.ab:
So Sir, is this a slip of your own grafting,
You are so prodigall?

sp.speaker: Ia
sp.ab: A slip Sir?

sp.speaker: Hen
sp.ab:
Yes,
A slip; or call it by the proper name
Your Bastard.

sp.speaker: Ia
sp.ab:
You are foul-mouth’d; do not provoke me,
I shall forget your Birth, if you proceed,
And use you, (as your manners do deserve) uncivilly.

sp.speaker: Hen
sp.ab:
So brave? pray you give me hearing,
Who am I Sir?

sp.speaker: Ia
sp.ab:
My elder Brother: One
That might have been born a fool and so reputed,
But that you had the luck to creep into
The world a yeare before me.

sp.speaker: Lean
sp.ab: Be more temperate.

sp.speaker: Ia
sp.ab:
I neither can nor will, unles se I learn it
By this example: let him use his harsh
Unsavoury reprehensions upon those
That are his hinds, and not on me. The Land
Our father left to him alone rewards him,
For being twelve moneths elder, let that be
Forgotten, and let his Parasites remember
One quality of worth or vertue in him
That may authorise him, to be a censurer
Of me, or of my manners, and I will
Acknowledge him for a tutor, til then, never

sp.speaker: Hen
sp.ab: From whom have you your meanes Sir?

sp.speaker: Ia
sp.ab:
From the will
Of my dead father; I am sure I spend not
Nor give’t upon your purse.

sp.speaker: Hen
sp.ab:
But will it hold out
Without my help?

sp.speaker: Ia
sp.ab:
I am sure it shall I’le sink else
For sooner I will seek aid from a whore,
Then a courtesie from you.

sp.speaker: Hen
sp.ab:
’Tis well; you are proud of
Your new Exchequer when you have cheated him
And worn him to the quick, I may be found
In the List of your acquaintance’

sp.speaker: Lea
sp.ab:
Pray you hold
And give me leave (my Lord) to say thus much
(And in mine own defence) I am no Gull
To be wrought on by perswasion: nor no Coward
To be beaten out of my meanes, but know to whom
And why I give or lend, and will do nothing
But what my reason warrants; you may be
As sparing as you please, I must be bold
To make use of mine own, without your licence.

sp.speaker: Ia
sp.ab:
’Pray thee let him alone, he is not worthy thy an[ger]
All that he do’s (Leandro) is for my good,
I think there’s not a Gentleman of Spain,
That ha’s a better steward, then I have of him.

sp.speaker: Hen
sp.ab: Your steward Sir?

sp.speaker: Ja
sp.ab:
Yes, and a provident one:
Why, he knowes I am given to large Expence,
And therefore layes up for me: could you believe els
That he, that sixteen years hath worne the yoke
Of barren wedlock, without hope of is sue,
(His Coffer’s full, his Lands, and Vineyards fruitfull)
Could be so sold to base, and forbid thrift,
As almost to deny himselfe, the meanes
And neces saries of life? Alas, he knowes
The Lawes of Spaine appoint me for his heire,
That all must come to me, if I out-live him,
(Which sure I must doe, by the course of Nature,)
And the as sistance of good Mirth, and Seck,
How ever you prove Melancholy.

sp.speaker: Hen
sp.ab:
If I live,
Thou dearly shalt repent this,

sp.speaker: Ja
sp.ab:
When thou art dead,
I am sure I shall not.

sp.speaker: Mil
sp.ab:
Now they begin to burn
Like oppos’d Meteors.

sp.speaker: Ars
sp.ab:
Give them line, and way,
My life for Don Jamie.

sp.speaker: Ja
sp.ab:
Continue still
The excellent Husband, and joyne Farme to Farme,
Suffer no Lordship, that in a cleare day
Falls in the prospect of your coveteous eye
To be an others; Forget you are a Grandee
Take use upon use, and cut the throats of heires
With cozening Mort-gages: rack your poore Tenants,
Till they looke like so many Skeletons
For want of Food; And when that Widowes curses,
The ruines of ancient Families, teares of Orphans
Have hurried you to the divell, ever remember
All was rak’d up, for me, (your thankfull Brother)
That will dance merrily upon your Grave,
And perhaps give a double Pistolet
To some poore needy Frier, to say a Masse
To keep your Ghost from walking.

sp.speaker: Hen
sp.ab:
That the Law
Should force me to endure this!

sp.speaker: Ia
sp.ab:
Verely,
When this shall come to passe (as sure it will)
If you can find a loope-hole, though in hell’
To looke on my behaviour, you shall see me
Ransack your Iron Chests, and once againe
Pluto’s flame-colour’d Daughter shall be free
To dominier in Taverns, Maskes, and Revells
As she was us’d before she was your Captive.
Me thinkes the meere conceipt of it, should make you
Goe home sick and distemper’d, if it do’s,
I’le send you a Doctor of mine owne, and after
Take order for your Funerall.

sp.speaker: Hen
sp.ab:
You have said, sir,
I will not fight with words, but deeds to tame you,
Rest confident I will, and thou shalt wish
This day thou hadst been dumb. ---

sp.speaker: Mil
sp.ab:
You have given him a heat.
But with your owne distemper.

sp.speaker: Ia
sp.ab:
Not a whit
Now he is from mine eye, I can be merry.
Forget the cause, and him: all plagues goe with him
Let’s talke of something els: what newes is stirring?
Nothing to pas se the time?

sp.speaker: Mil
sp.ab:
’Faith it is said
That the next Summer will determine much
Of that we long have talk’d of, touching the Wars.

sp.speaker: Lea
sp.ab:
What have we to doe with them? Let us discourse
Of what concerns our selves. ’Tis now in fashion
To have you Gallants set downe, in a Taverne,
What the Arch-Dukes purpose is the next spring & what
Defence my Lords (the States) prepare: what course
The Emperour takes against the encroching Turke,
And whither his Moony-Standards are design’d
For Persia, or Polonia: and all this
The wiser sort of State-Wormes seeme to know
Better then their owne Affaires: this is discourse
Fit for the Counsell it concerns; we are young,
And if that I might give the Theame, ’twere better
To talke of handsome women.

sp.speaker: Mil
sp.ab:
And that’s one,
Almost as generall.

sp.speaker: Ars
sp.ab:
Yet none agree
Who are the fairest.

sp.speaker: Lea
sp.ab:
Some prefer the French,
For their conceited Dressings: some the plump
Italian Bona-Robas, some the State
That ours observe; and I have heard one sweare,
(A merry friend of mine) that once in London,
He did enjoy the company of a Gamester
(A common Gamester too) that in one night
Met him th’Italian, French, and Spanish waies,
And ended in the Dutch; for, to coole her selfe,
She kiss’d him drunke in the morning.

sp.speaker: Ia
sp.ab:
Wee may spare
The travell of our tongues in forraigne Nations,
When in Corduba if you dare give credit
To my report (for I have seene her, Gallants)
There lives a woman) of meane birth too,
And meanly match’d) whose all-excelling Forme
Disdaines comparison with any She
That puts in for a faire one, and though you borrow
From every Country of the Earth the best
Of those perfections which the Clymat yeilds
To help to make her up, if put in Ballance,
This will weigh-downe the Scale.

sp.speaker: Lea
sp.ab: You talke of wonders.

sp.speaker: Ia
sp.ab:
She is indeed, a wonder, and so kept,
And, as the world deserv’d not to behold
What curious Nature made without a patterne,
Whose Copy she hath lost too, she’s shut up,
Sequestred from the world.

sp.speaker: Lea
sp.ab:
Who is the owner
Of such a Jem? I am fir’d.

sp.speaker: Ia
sp.ab:
One Bartolus,
A wrangling Advocate.

sp.speaker: Ars
sp.ab: A knave on Record.

sp.speaker: Mil
sp.ab:
I am sure he cheated me of the best part
Of my Estate.

sp.speaker: Ia
sp.ab:
Some Busines se calls me hence,
(And of importance) which denies me leisure
To give you his full character: In few words
(Though rich) he’s covetous beyond expres sion,
And to encrease his heape, will dare the Divell,
And all the plagues of darknesse: and to these
So jealous, as if you would paralell
Old Argus to him, you must multiply
His Eies and hundred times: of these, none sleepe.
He that would charme the heaviest lid, must hire
A better Mercurie, then Iove made use of:
Bles se your selves from the thought of him and her
For ’twill be labour lost: So farewell Signiors.---Exit.

sp.speaker: Ars
sp.ab: Leandro? in a dreame? wake man, for shame.

sp.speaker: Mil
sp.ab:
Trayned into fooles paradise with a tale
Of an imagin’d Forme,

sp.speaker: Lea
sp.ab:
Iamie is noble,
And with a forg’d Tale would not wrong his Friend,
Nor am I so much fired with lust as Envie,
That such a churl as Bartolus should reap
So sweete a har vest, half my State to any
To help me a share.

sp.speaker: Ars
sp.ab:
Tush do no hope for
Impos sibilities,

sp.speaker: Lea
Ars
sp.ab: Give it ’ore,

sp.speaker: Mil
sp.ab: I would not have thee fool’d

sp.speaker: Lea
sp.ab:
I have strange Engines
Fashioning here: and Bartolus on the Anville
Diswade me not but help me,

sp.speaker: Mil
sp.ab:
Take your fortune,
If you come off well; praise your wit, if not,
Expect to be the subject of our Laughter.Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Iac
sp.ab: You met Don Henrique.

sp.speaker: Oct
sp.ab: Yes:

sp.speaker: Iac
sp.ab:
What comfort bring you?
Speake cheerefully: how did my Letter worke?
On his hard temper? I am sure I wrot it,
So feelingly, and with the pen of sorrow,
That it must force Compunction,

sp.speaker: Oct
sp.ab:
You are cozen’d;
Can you with one hand prop a falling Tower?
Or with the other stop theraging maine,
When it breakes in on the usurped Shore?
Or any thing that is impos sible?
And then conclude that there is some way left,
To move him to compas sion.

sp.speaker: Iac
sp.ab:
Is there a Justice
Or thunder (my Octavio) and he
Not sunk unto the center?

sp.speaker: Oct
sp.ab:
Good Iacinta.
With your long practised patience beare afflictions,
And by provoking it call not on Heavens anger,
He did not onely scorne to read your Letter,
But (most inhumane as he is) he cursed you,
Cursed you most bitterly,Ascanio be ready.

sp.speaker: Iac
sp.ab:
The bad mans charity,
Oh that I could forget there were a Tye,
In me upon him! or the releife I seeke,
(If given) were bounty in him, and not debt,
Debt of a deere accompt!

sp.speaker: Oct
sp.ab:
Touch not that string,
Twill but encrease your Sorrow, and tame silence,
(The Balme of the oppres sed) which hitherto
Hath eas’d your grieved soule, and preserv’d your fame,
Must be your Surgeon still.

sp.speaker: Iac
sp.ab:
If the contagion
Of my misfortunes had not spread it self,
Upon my Son Ascanio, though my wants
Were centupli’d upon my self, I could be patient:
But he is so good, I so miserable,
His pious care his dutie, and obedience,
And all that can be wish’d for from a Son,
Discharg’d to me, and I, bard of all meanes,
To returne any scruple of the debt
I owe him as a Mother, is a Torment,
Too painefull to be borne.

sp.speaker: Oct
sp.ab:
I suffer with you,
In that; yet find in this as surance comfort,
High heavens ordaines (whose purposes cannot alter)

Children that pay obedience to their Parents,
Shall never beg their Bread.

sp.speaker: Iac
sp.ab:
Here comes our joy,
Where has my dearest been?

sp.speaker: Asc
sp.ab:
I had made (Mother)
A fortunate voyage and brought home rich prize,
In a few houres: the owners too contented,
From whom I tooke it. See heres Gold, good store too
Nay, pray you take it,

sp.speaker: Iac
sp.ab:
Mens Charities are so cold,
That if I knew not, thou wert made of Goodnes,
’Twould breed a jealousie in me by what meanes,
Thou cam’st by such a sum

sp.speaker: Asc
sp.ab:
Were it ill got,
I am sure it could not be employed so well,
As to relieve your wants. Some noble Friends,
(Rais’d by heavens mercy to me, not my merits)
Bestow’d it on me.

sp.speaker: Oct
Iac
sp.ab:
Buy thee brave Cloathes with it
And fit thee for a fortune, and leave us,
To our neces sities; why do’st thou weep?

sp.speaker: Asc
sp.ab:
Out of my feare, I have offended you;
For had I not, I am sure you are too kind,
Not to accept the offer of my service,
In which I am a gainer; I have heard
My tutor say of all aiereall foule
The Storke’s the Embleme of true pietie,
Because when age hath seiz’d upon her dam,
And made unfit for flight, the gratefull young one
Takes her upon his back, provides her foode,
Repaying so, her tender care of him,Hen: & Viol: be ready.
’Ere he was fit to fly, by bearing her:
Shall I then that have reason, and discourse
That tell me all I can doe is too litle,
Be more unnaturall then a silly Bird?
Or feed or cloth my selfe superfluously,
And know, nay see you want? holy Saints keepe me.

sp.speaker: Iac
sp.ab:
Can I be wretched,
And know my selfe the Mother to such Goodnes?

sp.speaker: Oct
sp.ab:
Come, let us drie our eyes, wee’ll have a Feast,
Thanks to our little Steward;

sp.speaker: Iac
sp.ab:
And in him,
Beleeve that we are rich.

sp.speaker: Asc
sp.ab:
I am sure I am,
While I have power to comfort you, and serve you.

sp.speaker: Viol
sp.ab:
Is it my fault, (Don Henrique) or my fate,
Wha’ts my offence? I came young to your Bed
I had a fruitfull Mother, and you met me,
With equall ardour in your May of blood;
And why then am I barren?

sp.speaker: Hen
sp.ab:
’Tis not in Man
To yield a reason for the will of Heaven,
Which is inscrutable.

sp.speaker: Viol
sp.ab:
To what use serve
Full fortunes, and the meaner sort of Bles sings,
When that, which is the Crowne of all our wishes,
The period of humane happines,
One only Child that may pos ses se what’s ours,
Is cruelly denide us?

sp.speaker: Hen
sp.ab:
’Tis the curse,
Of great Estates to want those Pledges which,
The poore are happy in: They in a Cottage,
With joy, behold the Modells of their youth,
And as their Roote decaies those budding Branches,
Sprout forth and flourish, to renew their age;
But this is the beginning not the end
To me, of, that misery against my will,
(Since Heaven denies us Is sue of our owne)
Must leave the fruit of all my care and travell
To an unthankfull Brother that insults,
On my Calamity.

sp.speaker: Viol
sp.ab:
I will rather choose,
A Bastard from the Hospitall and adopt him,
And nourish him, as mine owne.

sp.speaker: Hen
sp.ab:
Such an evasion
(My Violante) is forbid to us;
Happy the Romane State, where it was lawfull,
(If our owne Sonnes were vicious) to choose one
Out of a vertuous Stock, though of poore Parents,
And make him noble. But the Lawes of Spaine,
(Intending to preserve all ancient Houses)
Prevent such free elections; with this my Brothers
Too well acquainted and this makes him bold to
Reigne ‘ore me, as a Master,

sp.speaker: Viol
sp.ab:
I will fire
The Portion I brought with me, ‘ere he spend,
A Royall of it: No Quirck left? no Quiddit
That may defeate him?

sp.speaker: Hen
sp.ab:
Were I but confirmed,
That you would take the meanes I use, with patience,
As I must practise it with my dishonour,
I could lay levell with the earth his hopes
That soare above the clouds with expectation
To see me in my grave.

sp.speaker: Viol
sp.ab:
Effect but this
And our revenge shall be to us a Son
That shall inherit for us.

sp.speaker: Hen
sp.ab:
Do not repent
When ’tis too late.

sp.speaker: Viol
sp.ab:
I feare not what may fall
He disposes s’d that doe’s usurpe on all

div.stage: Enter Leandro (with a letter writ out) Milanes & Asernio

sp.speaker: Mil
sp.ab: Can any thing, but wonder?

sp.speaker: Lean
sp.ab:
Wonder on,
I am as ye see, and what will follow Gentlemen

sp.speaker: Ars
sp.ab:
Why dost thou put on this form? what can this do?
Thou lookest most sillily,

sp.speaker: Mil
sp.ab:
Like a young Clerk
A half pin’d-puppy that would write for a Royall.
Is this a commanding shape to win a Beautie?
To what use, what occasion?

sp.speaker: Lean
sp.ab:
Peace ye are fooles,
More silly then my out-side seems ye are ignorant
They that pretend to wonders must weave cunningly.

sp.speaker: Ars
sp.ab:
What manner of acces se can this get? or if gotten
What credit in her eyes?

sp.speaker: Lean
sp.ab: Will ye but leave me?

sp.speaker: Mil
sp.ab:
Me thinks a young man and a handsom Gentleman
(But sure thou art lunatick) me thinks a brave man
That would catch cunningly the beames of Beautie,
And so distribute’em unto his comfort,
Should like himself appeare, young, high, and buxom.
And in the brightest form.

sp.speaker: Lean
sp.ab:
Ye are cozen’d (Gentlemen)Lop: Diegoe be ready.
Neither doe I believe this, nor will follow it,
Thus I am, I will begin my voyage,
When you love, lanch it out in silks and velvets,
I le love in Serge, and will outgo your Sattins
To get upon my great horse and appeare.
The signe of such a man, and trot my measures,
Or fiddle out whole frosty nights (my friends)
Vnder the window while my teeth keep tune,
I hold no handsomnes se. Let me get in
There trot and fiddle where I may have faire play,

sp.speaker: Ars
sp.ab: But how get in?

sp.speaker: Lean
sp.ab:
Leave that to me, your patience,
I have some toyes here that I dare well trust to:
I have smelt a Vicar out they call him Lopez.
You are ne’re the nearer now,

sp.speaker: Mil
sp.ab: We do confes se it.

sp.speaker: Lean
sp.ab:
Weak simplemen this Vicar to this Lawyer
Is the most inward, Damon.

sp.speaker: Ars
sp.ab: What can this do?

sp.speaker: Mil
sp.ab: We know the fellow, and he dwells there.

sp.speaker: Lean
sp.ab: So.

sp.speaker: Ars
sp.ab:
A poore, thin theef: he help? he; hang the Vicar
Can reading of an — — preferre thee?

sp.speaker: Lean
sp.ab:
Thou art dead-sick in love, and hee’l pray for thee
Have patience (Gentlemen) I say this Vicar
This thing I say is all one with the Close Bartolus
(For so they call the Lawyer) or his nature
Which I have studied by relation;
And make no doubt I shall hit hansomly,
Will I work cunningly and home: understand me. Enter Lopez and Diego. Cross-hatched lines.
Next pray leave me, Leave me to my fortune
Difficilia pulchra, thats my Motto (Gentlemen)
I ’le win this Diamond from the rock and weare her
Or — —

sp.speaker: Mil
sp.ab: Peace, the Vicar: send ye a full sail, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ars
sp.ab:
There’s your Confes sor, but what shal be your pen-
(nance? exit lea.
A fools head if I fail and so forsake me.
You shall heare from me daily.

sp.speaker: Mil
sp.ab: We will be ready

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab: Thin world indeed:

sp.speaker: Lean
sp.ab:
I’le let him breathe and mark him:
No man would think a stranger as I am
Should reap any great commodity from his pigbelly,

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab: Poore stirring for poore Vicars,

sp.speaker: Diego
sp.ab: And poore Sextons.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
We pray and pray, but to no purpose
Those that enjoy our Lands, choak our Devotions.
Our poore thin stipends make us arrant dunces,

sp.speaker: Diego
sp.ab:
If you live miserably, how shall we do (Master?)
That are fed onely with the sound of prayers?
We rise and ring the Bells to get good stomacks.
And must be fain to eat the ropes with reverence,

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab: When was there a Christning (Diego?)

sp.speaker: Dieg
sp.ab:
Not this ten weekes:
Alas, they have forgot to get children ( Master)
The Warres, the Seas, and usurie undoe us,
Takes off our minds, our edges, blunts our plough-shares,
They eat nothing here, but herbs, & get nothing green
(sauce:
There are some poore Labourers, that perhaps
Once in seven yeare, with helping one another,
Produce some few pind––Butter––prints, that scarce hold
The christning neither.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
Your Gallants, they get Honour,
A strange fantasticall Birth, to defraud the Vicar,
And the Camp Christens their Is sues, or the Curtizans,
’Tis a lewd time.

sp.speaker: Die
sp.ab:
They are so hard-hearted here too,
They will not dye, there’s nothing got by Burialls.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
Diego, the Ayre’s too pure, they cannot perish:
To have a thin Stipend, and an everlasting Parish,
Lord what a torment ’tis!

sp.speaker: Die
sp.ab:
Good sensible Master,
You are allow’d to pray against all weathers,
(Both foule, and faire, as you shall find occasion)
Why not against all ayres?

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
That’s not i’th’ Canons,
I would it had, ’tis out of our way forty pence.

sp.speaker: Di
sp.ab:
’Tis strange, they are starv’d too, yet they wil not die
(here,
They will not Earth: a good stout plague amongst ’um,
Or halfe a dozen new fantasticall Fevers
That would turne up their heeles by whole-sale (Master)
And take the Doctors too, in their grave Counsells,
How merrily would my Bells goe then?

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
Peace Diego,
The Doctors are our friends, let’s please them well,
For though they kill but slow, they are certaine (Diego)
We must remove into a muddy Ayre,
A most contagious Clymat.

sp.speaker: Die
sp.ab:
We must certaine,
An ayre that is the nursery of Agues,
Such Agues (Master) that will shake mens soules out,
Ne’re stay for Pos sets, nor good old wives’ plaisters.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab: Gowts and dead Palsies.

sp.speaker: Die
sp.ab:
The dead doe’s well at all times,
Yet Gowts will hang an ars se a long time (Master)
The Pox, or English Surfets if we had ’em;
Those are rich Marle, they make a Church-yard fat,
And make the Sexton sing, they never mis se, Sir.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
Then Wills and Funerall Sermons come in season,
And Feasts that makes us frolicke.

sp.speaker: Die
sp.ab: Would I could see’ em.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
And though I weepe i’th’ Pulpit for my Brother,
Yet (Diego) here I laugh.

sp.speaker: Di
sp.ab: The cause requires it.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab: Since people left to die I am dunce (Diego.)

sp.speaker: Die
sp.ab: ’Tis a strange thing, I have forgot to dig too.

sp.speaker: Lea
sp.ab: A pretious pair of youths; I must make toward ’em

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
Who’s that? look out it seemes he would speak to
(us.)
I hope a Marriage or some Wil to make (Diego)

sp.speaker: Dieg
sp.ab: My friend, your busines se?

sp.speaker: Lea
Lop
sp.ab:
And bles se you also,
He beares a promising face, there’s some hope toward.

sp.speaker: Lea
sp.ab: I have a Letter to your worship.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
Well Sir,
From whence I pray you?

sp.speaker: Lea
sp.ab:
From Nova Hispania, Sir,
And from an ancient friend of yours.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
’Tis well (Sir)
’Tis very well: the divell a-one I know there.

sp.speaker: Die
sp.ab:
Take heed of a Snap (Sir) has a cozening coun-
(tenance,
I doe not like his way.

div.sp:
Lop
Let him goe forward.
Cantabit Vacuus, They that have nothing feare nothing,
All I have to loose (Diego) is my learning,
And when he has gotten that, he may put it in a Nut shell,
Letter Read
Signor Lopez,
Since my arrivall from Cordova to these
parts, I have written divers Letters unto you but as
yet received no Answer of any (Good and very good) And
although so great a forgetfulnes se might cause a want in my
due correspondence yet the desire I have still to serve you
must more prevaile with me (Better and better: the divell
a man know I yet) and therefore with the present occasion
offered I am willing to crave a continuance of the favours,
which I have heretofore received from you and doe recom-
mend my Son Leandro the Bearer to you with request
that he may be admitted in that Universitie till such time
as I shall arive at home; his studies he will make you ac-
quainted withall: This kindnes se shall supply the want of your
slacknes se: And so heaven keep you. Yours
Alonzo Tiveria
Alonzo Tiveria, very well,
A very ancient friend of mine I take it,
For till this houre I never heard his Name, yet.

sp.speaker: Lea
sp.ab: You looke (Sir) as if ye had forgot my Father.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
No, no, I look as I would remember him,
For that I never remembered, I cannot forget (Sir)
Alonzo Tiveria.

sp.speaker: Lea
sp.ab: The same (Sir.)

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab: And now i’th’ Indies?

sp.speaker: Lea
sp.ab: Yes.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
He may be any where,
For ought I consider.

sp.speaker: Lea
sp.ab:
Thinke againe (Sir)
You were Students both at one time in Salamanca,
And, as I take it, Chamber-fellowes.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab: Ha?

sp.speaker: Lea
sp.ab: Nay, sure you must remember.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab: Would I could.

sp.speaker: Lea
sp.ab: I have heard him say, you were Gos sips too.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
Very likely,
You did not heare him say, to whom? for we Students
May often-times over-reach our memories,
Do’st thou remember (Diego) this same Signiour?
Thou hast been mine these twenty yeares.

sp.speaker: Di
sp.ab:
Remember?
Why, this Fellow would make ye mad: Nova Hispania?
And Signiour Tiveria? what are these?
He may as well name ye Friends out of Cataya
Take heed, I beseech your worship: doe you heare, (my
(friend?
You have no Letters for me?

sp.speaker: Lea
sp.ab:
Not any Letter,
But I was charged to doe my Fathers love
To the old honest Sexton Diego; are you he (Sir?)

sp.speaker: Di
sp.ab:
Ha? have I friends, and know ’em not? my name is
Diego,
But if either I remember you or your Father
Or Nova Hispania (I was never there Sir)
Or any kindred that you have--for heaven-sake, Master,
Let’s cast about a little, and consider,
We may dreame out our time.

sp.speaker: Lea
sp.ab:
It seemes I am deceiv’d (Sir) Yet
31
Yet; that you are Don Lopez, all men tell me,
That Curat here, and have bin some time (sir)
And you the Sexton Diego, such I am sent too,
The Letter tells as much: may be they are dead,
And you of the like name succeed: I thank ye gentlemen,
Ye have done honestly, in telling truth,
I might have bin forward els. For that Lopez
That was my Fathers friend, I had a charge,
(A charge of Money) to deliver (Gentlemen)
Five hundred Duckets, a poore small gratuity,
But since you are not he, good sir, let me thinke,
I pray ye be patient.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
Pray ye stay a little,
Nay, let me remember, I beseech ye stay, Sir.

sp.speaker: Die
sp.ab:
An honest noble friend, that sends so lovingly;
An old friend too; I shall remember sure, Sir.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab: Thou sayst true Diego.

sp.speaker: Di
sp.ab:
’Pray ye consider quickly,
Doe, doe, by any meanes, me thinkes already
A grave staid gentleman comes to my memory.

sp.speaker: Lea
sp.ab: He’s old indeed, sir.

sp.speaker: Di
sp.ab:
With a goodly white Beard,
(For now he must be so: I know he must be)
Signior Alonzo, (Master.)

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab: I begin to have him.

sp.speaker: Di
sp.ab: ’Has bin from hence, about some twenty years (sir.)

sp.speaker: Lea
sp.ab: Som five and twenty (sir.)

sp.speaker: Di
sp.ab:
You say most true (sir)
Just to an houre; ’tis now just five and twenty,
A fine straite timber’d man, and a brave souldier,
He married: let me see, —

sp.speaker: Lea
sp.ab: De Castro’s Daughter.

sp.speaker: Di
sp.ab: The very same.

sp.speaker: Lea
sp.ab:
Thou art a very Rascall,
De Castro is the Turke to thee, or any thing :
The Money rubbs ’em into strange remembrances,
For as many Duckets more they wou d remember Adam.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
Give me your hand, you are welcome to your
countrey,
Now I remember plainly, manifestly,
As freshly, as if yesterday I had seene him,
Most heartily welcome, sinfull that I am,
Most sinfull man, why should I loose this Gentleman ?
This loving old Companion ? we had all one soule, sir,
He dwelt here hard by, at a handsome—

sp.speaker: Lea
sp.ab:
Farme sir,
You say most true.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
Alonzo Tiveria;
Lord, Lord, that time should play the treacherous knave
thus
Why, he was the onely friend, I had in Spaine (sir)
I knew your Mother too, a handsome Gentlewoman,
She was married very young: I married ’em:
I doe remember now the Maskes and Sports then,
The Fire-workes, and the fine delights; good faith, sir,
Now I looke in your face whose eies are those Diego?
Nay, if he be not just Alonzo’s picture—

sp.speaker: Lea
sp.ab: Lord how I blush for these two impundents?

sp.speaker: Di
sp.ab: Well Gentleman, I thinke your name’s Leandro;

sp.speaker: Lea
sp.ab:
It is indeed (sir)
Gra’-mercy Letter thou hadst never knowne els.

sp.speaker: Di
sp.ab:
I have dandled ye, and kist ye and plaid with ye
A hundred, and a hundred times, and danc’d ye,
And swong ye in my Bell-ropes, ye lov’d swinging.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab: A sweet Boy.

sp.speaker: Lea
sp.ab:
Sweet lying knaves,
What would these doe for thousands?

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
A wondrous sweet Boy then it was, see now
Bar: & Ama: be ready Time that consumes us, shoots him up still sweeter.
How do s the noble Gentleman? how fares he?
When shall wee see him? when will he bles se his Country?

sp.speaker: Lea
sp.ab:
O, very shortly, sir, till his returne,
He has sent me over to your charge.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
And welcome,
Nay, you shall know you are welcome to your friend, sir,

sp.speaker: Lea
sp.ab:
And to my Study (sir) which must be the Law,
To further which, he would entreat your care
To plant me in the favour of some man
That’s expert in that knowledge: for his paines
I have three hundred Duckets more: For my Diet,
Enough (sir) to defray me: which I am charged
To take still, as I use it, from your custodie,
I have the money ready, and I am weary.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
Sit down, sit down, and once more ye are most wel
come
The Law you have hit upon most happily,
Here is a Master in that Art, Bartolus,
A neighbour by, to him I will preferre ye,
A learned man, and my most loving Neighbour,
I’ll doe ye faithfull service (sir.)

sp.speaker: Di
sp.ab:
He’s an As se,
And so wee’ll use him; he shall be a Lawyer.

sp.speaker: Lo
sp.ab:
But if ever he recover this mony again: before Diego.
And get some pretty pittance: my Pupill’s hungry.

sp.speaker: Lea
sp.ab: Pray ye Sir, unlade me.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
I’le refresh ye Sir;
When ye want, you know your Exchequer.

sp.speaker: Lea
sp.ab: If all this get me but acces se, I am happy.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab: Come, I am tender of ye,

sp.speaker: Lea
sp.ab:
I’ll goe with ye,
To have this Fort betray’d these fooles must sliece me.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
My Amaranta, a retir’d sweet life,
Private and close, and still, and houswifely,
Becomes a Wife, sets off the grace of a woman
At home to be beleev’d both young, and handsome,
As Lillies that are casde in christall Glas ses,
Makes up the wonder: shew it abroad. ’tis stale,
And still and the more eyes cheapen it ’tis more slubberd,
And what needs windowes open to inviting?
Or evening Tarresses, to take opinions?More be rea
When the most wholsome Ayre (my wife) blowes inward,
When good thoughts are the noblest Campanions,
And old chast stories (wife) the best discourses;
But why doe I talke thus, that you know thy nature?

sp.speaker: Ama
sp.ab:
You know your own disease: distrust, & jealousies;
And those two, give these Les sons, not good meaning,
What triall is there of my honestie,
When I am mew’d at home? to what end, Husband,
Serves all the vertvous thoughts, and chast behaviours
Without their uses? Then they are known most excellent
When, by their contraries they are set off, and burnish’d,
If ye both hold me faire, and chast, and vertuous,
Let me goe feareles se out, and win that greatnes se;
These seeds grow not in Shades, and conceal’d places
Set ’em i’th’ heat of all, then they rise glorious.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab: Peace, you are too loude.

sp.speaker: Ama
sp.ab:
You are too covetous,
If that be rank’d a vertue, you have a rich one, Set
32
Set me (like other Lawyers wives) off handsomely,
Attended as I ought, and as they have it,
My Coach, my people, and my handsome women,
My will, in honest things.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab: Peace Amaranta:

sp.speaker: Ama
sp.ab:
They have content, rich clothes, and that se-
(cures’ em
Bindes, to their carefull Husbands, their observance,
They are merry, ride abroad, meet, laugh,

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab: Thou shalt too:

sp.speaker: Ama
sp.ab:
And freely may converse with proper Gentlemen,
Suffer temptations daily to their honour.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
You are now too far again: thou shalt have any
thing,
Let me but lay up for a handsome Office,
And then my Amaranta—

sp.speaker: Ama
sp.ab:
Here’s a thing now,
Ye place as pleasure to me: all my retinue,
My Chamber-maid, my Kitchin-maid, my friend,
And what she failes in, I must doe my selfe.
A foyle to set my Beauty off, I thank ye,
You will place the Devill next for a Companion,

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
No more such words (good wife)
What would you have (Maid?)

sp.speaker: Moor
sp.ab:
Master Curate, and the Sexton, & a stranger (sir)
Attend to speake with your worship.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab: A stranger?

sp.speaker: Ama
sp.ab:
You had best to be jealous of the man you know
not.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab: ’Pree ’thee no more of that.

sp.speaker: Ama
sp.ab:
’Pray ye goe out to ’em,
That will be safest for ye, I am well here,
I onely love your peace, and serve like a slave for it.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
No, no, thou shalt not; ’tis some honest Client
Rich and litigious, the Curate has brought to me,
Pre’thee goe in (my Duck) I’ll but speake to ’em,
And returne instantly.

sp.speaker: Ama
sp.ab:
I am commanded,
One day you will know my sufferance.——Exit.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
And reward it.
So, so, fast bind, fast find; Come in my Neighbours,
My loving Neighbours pray ye come in, ye are welcome,

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab: Bles se your good reverence.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
Good-day, good Master Curate,
And neighbour Diego, welcome: what’s your busines se?
And ’pray ye be short (good friends) the time is pretious,
Welcome, good sir.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
To be short then with your Mastership,
(For I know your severall houres, are full of busines se)
We have brought ye this young-man, of honest parents,
And of an honest face.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
It seemes so (Neighbours)
But to what end?

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
To be your Pupill (Sir)
Your Servant, if you please.

sp.speaker: Lea
sp.ab:
I have travell’d far, sir.
To seeke a worthy man,

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
Alas, good Gentleman,
I am a poore man, and a private too,
Unfit to keep a Servant of your Reckoning;
My house a little Cottage, and scarce able
To hold my selfe, and those poore few live under it;
Besides, you must not blame me Gentleman,
If I were able to receive a Servant,
To be a little scrupulous of his dealing
For in these times—

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
’Pray let me answer that (sir)
Here is five hundred Duckets, to secure him,
He cannot want (sir) to make good his credit,
Good gold, and coyne.

sp.speaker: Bar
Lea
sp.ab:
And for I have a ripe mind to the Law (sir)
(In which I understand you live a Master)
The least poore corner in your house, poore Bed (sir)
(Let me not seeme intruding to your Worship)
With some Books to instruct me, and your Counsell,
Shall I rest most content with: other Acquaintance
Then your grave presence, and the grounds of Law
I dare not covet, nor I will not seeke (sir)
For surely mine owne nature desires privacie.
Next, for your monthly paines (to shew my thanks,)
I doe proportion out some twenty Duckets;
As I grow riper, more: three hundred now (sir)
To shew my love to learning, and my Master,
My diet, I’ll defray too, without trouble.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab: Note but his mind to learning.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
I do strangely, yes, and I like it too, thankes to his
(money.

sp.speaker: Di
sp.ab: Would he would live with me, and learn to dig too.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab: A wondrous modest man (sir.)

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
So it seemes,
His deare love to his Studie must be nourish’d
Neighbour, he’s like to prove.

sp.speaker: Lop
Bar
sp.ab: Come hither;

sp.speaker: Die
sp.ab:
An honester young man, your worship ne’re kept,
But he is too bashfull—

sp.speaker: Bar
Lea
sp.ab:
Any thing (sir)
That’s dry, and wholesome: I am no bred-wanton.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
Then I receive you: but I must desire ye
To keep within your confines.

sp.speaker: Lea
sp.ab:
Ever sir,
There’s the Gold, and ever be your servant,
Take it and give me Bookes: may I but prove (sir)
According to my wish, and these shall multiply.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
Do, study hard, pray ye take him in, and settle him,
He’s onely fit for you; Shew him his Cell (sir.)

sp.speaker: Di
sp.ab:
Take a good heart; and when ye are a cunning Law
yer,
I’le sell my Bells, and you shall prove it lawfull,

sp.speaker: Ba
sp.ab: Come, sir, with me: neighbors I thank your diligence.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab: I’l come sometimes, and crack a case with ye.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab: Welcome—

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
Here’s mony got with ease: here, spend that jovially,
And pray for the Foole, the Founder.

sp.speaker: Die
sp.ab:
Many more Fooles
I heartily pray may follow his example,
Lawyers, or Lubbers, or of what condition, And
F 33 Jamy Mill: arse be ready.
And many such sweet friends in Nova Hispania.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
It will do well; Let ’em but send their moneys,
Come from what quarter of the world, I care not,
I’ll know ’em instantly; nay I’ll be a kin to ’em;
I cannot mis se a man, that sends me money:
Let him Law there ? long as his Duckets last, Boy,
I’ll grace him, and prefer him.

sp.speaker: Die
sp.ab:
I’ll turn Trade (Master) and now live by the living,
Let the dead stinke, ’tis a poore stinking Trade.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
If the young Foole now
Should chance to chop upon his faire Wife (Diego.)

sp.speaker: Die
sp.ab:
And handle her Case (Master) that’s a law point,
A point would make him start, and put on his Spectacles
A hidden point, were worth the canvas sing.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
Now surely, surely, I should love him (Diego)
And love him heartily: nay, I should love my selfe,
Or any thing that had but that good fortune,
For to say truth the Lawyer is a dog-bolt,
An arrant worme: And through I call him worshipfull,
I wish him a canoniz’d Cuckhold (Diego)
Now, if my youth doe dub him—

sp.speaker: Di
sp.ab: He is too demure (sir.)

sp.speaker: Lopez
sp.ab: If he do sting her home.

sp.speaker: Die
sp.ab:
There’s no such matter,
The woman was not borne to so much bles sednes se
He has no heate: study consumes his oyle (Master,)

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
Let’s leave it to the will of Fate, aud presently)
Over a cup of lustie Sack, let’s prophecie.
I am like a man that dreampt he was an Emperour,
Come Diego, hope, & whilst he lasts, we’ll lay it on.Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Jam
sp.ab: Angelo, Millanes, did you see this wonder?

sp.speaker: Mil
sp.ab: Yes, yes.

sp.speaker: Jam
sp.ab: And you Arsenio?Servant be ready.

sp.speaker: Ar
sp.ab:
Yes he’s gon (Sir)
Strangely disguis’d, he’s set upon his voyage.
Love guide his thoughts: he’s a brave honest fellow,
Sit close Don Lawyer, ô that arrant knave now,
How he will stinke, will smoake againe, will burst:
He’s the most arrant Beast.

sp.speaker: Mil
sp.ab: He may be more beast.

sp.speaker: Ja,
sp.ab:
Let him beare six, and six, that all may blaze him,
The villany he has sowed into my Brother,bar: & Ama be
And from his State, the Revenue he has reach’d at:
Pay bim, my good Leandro, take my praiers.

sp.speaker: Ar
sp.ab: And all our wishes plough with his fine white heifer.

sp.speaker: Ja
sp.ab:
Marke him (my deare Friend) for a famous Cuckold,
Let it out-live his Bookes, his paines, and heare me,
The more he seeks to smother it with Justice,Enter a
Let it blaze out the more: what news Andrea?Servant. Cross-hatched lines.

sp.speaker: Andr
sp.ab:
Newes I am both to tell ye but I am charg’d (Sir)
Cross-hatched lines. Your Brother layes a strict command upon ye,
No more to know his house, upon your danger(ready
I am sorry (Sir.)

sp.speaker: Jam
sp.ab:
’Faith never be: I am glad on’t,
He keepes the house of pride, and foolery:
I meane to shun it: so returne my Answer,
Twill shortly spëw him out; Come, let’s be merry,
And lay our heads together, carefully
How we may helpe our friend; and let’s lodge neare him,
Be still at hand: I would not for my patrimony,
But he should crown his Lawyer a learned Monster,
Come, let’s away I am stark mad till I see him.Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Amar
sp.ab:
Why, will ye bring men in, and yet be jealous?
Why will ye lodge a young man, a man able,
And yet repine?

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
He shall not trouble thee (Sweet)
A modest poore slight thing, did I not tell thee
He was onely given to the Booke, and for that
How royally he paies? finds his owne meat too.

sp.speaker: Am
sp.ab:
I will not have him here: I know your coutses,
And what fits you will fall into of madnes se.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab: Y’faith, I will not Wife,

sp.speaker: Am
sp.ab: I will not try ye,

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
He comes not neare thee: shall not dare to tread
Within thy Lodgings, in an old out-Roome
Where Logs, and Coles were layd.ser: be ready

sp.speaker: Am
sp.ab: Now ye lay fire; Fire to consume your quiet.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
Didst thou know him,
Thou wouldst thinke as I doe: he disquiet thee?
Thou mayst weare him next thy heart, & yet not warme
(him
His mind (poore man) ’s o’th’ Law, how to live after,
And not on lewdnes se: on my conscience
He knowes not how to looke upon a woman
More then by reading what Sex she is.

sp.speaker: Am
sp.ab: I doe not like it (Sir.)

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
Do’st thou not see (Foole)
What presents he sends hourely in his gratefulnes se?
What delicate meates?

sp.speaker: Am
sp.ab:
You had best trust him at your Table,
Doe and repent it, doe.Amaranta be ready

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
If thou be’st willing,
By my troth, I thinke ye might come, he’s so modest,
He never speakes: here’s part of that he gave me,
He’ll eat but halfe a dozen bits, and rise immediatly,
Even as he eats, he studies: he’ll not disquiet thee,
Doe as thou pleasest (Wife.)Cross-hatched lines.

sp.speaker: Am
sp.ab: What means this Wood-cocke?Knock within.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
Retire (Sweet) there’s one knocks: come in, your bu-
(sines se.

sp.speaker: Ser
sp.ab:
My Lord, Don Henrique, would entreat ye, Sir,Lean be re[ady]
To come immediatly, and speake with him,
He has busines se of some moment.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
I’ll attend him,
I must be gon: I pre’thee thinke the best (wife)
At my returne, I’ll tell thee more, good morrow;
Sir, keep ye close, and study hard: an houre hence
ll read a new Case to ye:— Exit. Leandro within.

sp.speaker: Lean
sp.ab: I’ll be ready.

sp.speaker: Amar
sp.ab:
So many hundred Duckets to ly scurvily?
And learne the pelting law? this sounds but slenderly,
But very poorely: I would see this fellow
Very faine see him, how he lookes: I will find
To what end, and what study: there’s a place:
I’ll goe o’th’ other side, and take my Fortune;Cross-hatched lines.
I think there is a window.

sp.speaker: Lean
sp.ab:
He’s gone out
Now, if I could but see her: she is not this way:
How nastily he keepes his house? my Chamber,
If I continue long, will choak me up,
It is so damp: I shall be mortifide
For any woman, if I stay a moneth here:
I’ll in, and strike my Lute, that sound may call her.

sp.speaker: Ama
sp.ab:
He keeps very close: Lord, how I long to see him:
A lute strooke handsomely, a voice too; I’ll heare that:
These Verses are no Law, they sound too sweetly,
Now I am more desirous.

sp.speaker: Lea
sp.ab: ’Tis she certain.

sp.speaker: Am
sp.ab: What’s that that peeps?

sp.speaker: Lea
sp.ab: O, admirable face!

sp.speaker: Am
sp.ab: Sure ’tis the man.

sp.speaker: Lea
sp.ab: I will goe out a little.

sp.speaker: Am
sp.ab:
Hee lookes not like a foole, his face is noble:
How still he stands?

sp.speaker: Lea
sp.ab:
I am strucken dumb, with wonder,
Sure, all the Excellence of Earth dwells here.

sp.speaker: Am
sp.ab:
How pale he looks? yet how his eies like torches,
Fling their beams round: how manly his face shewes?
He comes on: surely he will speak: he is made most hand-
This is no Clerk behaviour; Now I have seen ye, (somly:
I’l take my time: husbad, ye have brought home tinder.

sp.speaker: Lea
sp.ab:
Sure she has transform’d me,
I had forgot my tongue cleane,
I never saw a face yet, but this rare one,
But I was able boldly to encounter it,
And speak my mind, my lips were lock upon me,
This is divine, and onely serv’d with reverence;
O most faire cover, of a hand far fairer,
Thou bles sed Innocence, that guards that whiteness,
Live next my heart. I am glad I have got a relick, A noise
A relick when I pray to it, may work wonders. within.
Harke, there’s some noyse: I must retire againe.
This bles sed Apparition, makes me happy;
I’ll suffer, and I’ll sacrifice my substance,
But I’ll enjoy: now softly to my Kennell.

sp.speaker: Hen
sp.ab: You know my cause sufficiently?

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab: I doe (Sir.)

sp.speaker: Hen
sp.ab:
And though it will impaire my honesty,
And strike deep at my Credit, yet (my Bartolus)
There being no other evasion left to free me
From the vexation of my spightfull Brother,
That most insultingly raignes over me,
I must and will goe forward.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
Doe (my Lord)
And looke not after credit, we shall cure that,
Your bended honestie, we shall set right (Sir)
We Surgeons of the Law, doe desperate cures (Sir)
And you shall see how heartily I’ll handle it:
Marke how I’ll knock it home: be of good cheare (Sir)
You give good Fees, and those beget good Causes,
The prerogative of your crownes will carry the matter,
(Carry it sheere) The As sistant sits to morrow,
And he’s your friend, your monied men love naturally,
And as your love are cleare, so are your Causes.

sp.speaker: Hen
sp.ab: He shall not want for that.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
No, no, he must not,
Line your Cause warmly (Sir) the times are Aguish,
That holds a Plea in heart; hand the penurious,
Their Causes (like their purses) have poore Is sues.

sp.speaker: Hen
sp.ab: That way, I was ever bountifull.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
’Tis true (Sir)
That makes ye fear’d, forces the Snakes to kneele to ye,
Live full of money, and supply the Lawyer,
And take your choice of what mans lands you please (Sir)
What pleasures, or what profits; what revenges,
They are all your owne: I must have witnes ses
Enough, and ready.

sp.speaker: Hen
sp.ab: You shall not want (my Bartolus.)

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
Substantiall fearless soules, that wil swear suddenly,
That will sweare any thing.

sp.speaker: Hen
sp.ab: They shall sweare truth too.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
That’s no great matter: for varietie
They may sweare truth, els ’tis not much look’d after:
I will serve Proces se, presently, and strongly
Upon your Brother, and Octavio,
Jacintha, and the Boy; provide your proofes (Sir)
And set ’em fairely off, be sure of Witnes ses,
Though they cost money, want no store of witnes ses,
I have seen a handsome Cause, so fowly lost (Sir,)
So beastly cast away for want or Witnes ses.

sp.speaker: Hen
sp.ab: There shall want nothing.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
Then be gone, be provident,
Send to the Judge, a secret way: you have me,
And let him understand the heart.

sp.speaker: Hen
sp.ab: I shall (Sir.)

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
And feele the pulses strongly beat, I’ll study,
And at my houre, but mark me, goe, be happy,
Goe, and beleeve i’th’Law.

sp.speaker: Hen
sp.ab: I hope ’twill helpe me.

div.stage: Enter Lopez, Diego, and foure Parishioners and Singers.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
Nea’r talke to me, I will not stay amongst ye,
Debaushe’d and ignorant lazie knaves I found ye,
And fooles I leave ye, I have taught these twenty yeares,
Preacht spoon-meat to ye, that a child might swallow,
Yet ye are Block-heads still: what should I say to ye?
Ye have neither faith, nor money left to save ye,
Am I fit companion for such Beggers?
If the Shepheard will suffer the sheep to be scab’d (Sir)

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab: No, no, ye are rotten.

sp.speaker: Di
sp.ab: Would they were, for my sake.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
I have nointed ye, and tar’d ye with my doctrine,
And yet the murren sticks to ye, yet ye are mangy,
I will avoid ye.

’Pray ye (Sir) be not angry,
In the pride of your new Cas sock, doe not part with us,
We doe acknowledge ye a carefull Curat,
And one that seldome troubles us with Sermons,
A short slice of a Reading serves us (Sir)
We doe acknowledge ye a quiet Teacher,
Before You’ll vex your Audience, you’ll sleep with ’em,
And that’s a loving thing.

We grant ye (Sir)
The onely benefactor to our Bowling,
To all our merry Sports, the first provoker,
And at our Feasts, we know there is no reason,
But you that edifie us most, should eat most.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
I will not stay for all of this, ye shall know me
A man borne to a more beseeming fortune
Then ringing all-in, to a rout of Dunces.

We will increase your Tithes, you shall have Egs too,
Though they may prove most dangerous to our Is sues.

I am a Smith; yet thus far out of my love
You shall have the tenth horse I prick, to pray for,
I am sure I prick five hundred in a yeare (Sir.

I am a Cooke, a man of dride conscience,
et thus far I relent: you shall have tith porrage.

Your stipend shal be rais’d (good neighbour Die
go

sp.speaker: Di
sp.ab:
Would ye have me speak for ye? I am more angry
Ten times more vex’d, not to be pacified:
No, there be other places for poore Sextons
Places of profit (Friends) fine stirring places,
And people that know how to use our Offices,
Know what they were made for: I speak for such Capons?
Ye shall find the Key o’th’ Church,
Under the doore (Neighbours,) You
F2 35
You may goe in, and drive away the dawes.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
My Surples se, with one sleeve, you shall find there,
For to that dearth of Linnen, you have driven me;
And the old Cutworke Cope, that hangs by gymitrie:
’Pray ye turne em carefully, they are very tender:
The remnant of the Books, lie where they did (Neigh
bours
Half puft away with the Church-wardens pipings.
Such smoaky zeales they have against hard places,
The poore-mans Box is there too: if ye find any thing
Besides the posie, and that halfe rub’d out too,
For feare it should awake too much charitie
Give it to pious uses, that is, spend it:

sp.speaker: Die
sp.ab:
The Bell-ropes, they are strong enough to hang ye,
So we bequeath ye to your destiny.
Pray ye be not so hastie.

sp.speaker: Di
sp.ab:
I’ll speake a proud word to ye,
Would ye have us stay?
We doe most hearilty pray ye.
I’ll draw as mighty drinke (Sir.)

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
A strong motive,
The stronger still the more ye come unto me.
And I’ll send for my Daughter:

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
This may stir too:
The Madien is of age, and must be edified.

You shall have any thing: loose our learned Vicar?
And our most constant friend; honest deare Diego?

sp.speaker: Di
sp.ab:
Yet all this will not do: I’ll tell ye (Neighbours)
And tell ye true: if ye will have us stay,
If you will have the comforts of our companies,
You shall be bound to doe us right in these points,
You shall be bound, and this the obligation,
Dy when ’tis fit, that we may have fit duties
And doe not seeke to draw—out our undoings,
Marry tryde women, that are free and fruitfull,
Get children in abundance, for your Christnings,
Or suffer to be got, ’tis equall justice,

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
Let Weddings, Christnings, Churchings, Funerals,
And merry Gos sippings goe round, go round still,
Round as a Pig, that we may find the profit.

sp.speaker: Die
sp.ab:
And let your old men fall sick handsomely:
And dy immediatly, their Sonnes may shoot up:
Let women dy oth’sullens too, ’tis naturall,
But be sure their Daughters be of age first,
That they may stock us still: your queazie young wives
That perish undeliver’d, I am vext with,
And vext abundantly, it much concerns me,
There’s a childes buriall lost, looke that be mended.

sp.speaker: Lo
sp.ab:
Let ’em be brought to bed, then dy when they please,
These things considered (Country-men) and sworne to
All these, and all our sports againe, and gambolls.

We must dy, and we must live, and we’ll be merry,
Every man shall be rich by one another.

We are here tomorrow, and gone today: for my part
If getting children can be-friend my Neighbours,
I’ll labour hard but I will fill your Font ( Sir.)

I have a Mother now, and an old Father,
They are as sure your own, within these two moneths—

My Sister must be prayd for too, she is desperate,
Desperate in love.Arseno & Millanes be ready

sp.speaker: Die
sp.ab:
Keepe, desperate men farre from her,
Then ’twill goe hard: doe you see how melancholy?
Doe you marke the man? do you profes se ye love him?
And would doe any thing to stay his fury?
And are ye unprovided to refresh him,
To make him know your loves? fie Neighbours,

We’ll doe any thing, Bar & ready on the table Dance be ready
We have brought Musick to appease his spirit,
And the best Song we’ll give him.

sp.speaker: Die
sp.ab:
’Pray ye sit down (Sir)
They know their duties now, and they stand ready
To tender their best mirth.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
’Tis well, proceed Neighbours,
I am glad I have brought ye to understand good manners,
Ye had Puritan hearts a-while, spurn’d at all pastimes,
But I see some hope now.Dance. Cross-hatched lines.

sp.speaker: Die
sp.ab: We are set proceed Neighbours.

sp.speaker: Ars
sp.ab: (it?

sp.speaker: Ars
sp.ab: What ayles this Priest? how highly the thing takes

sp.speaker: Mi
sp.ab:
Lord how it looks? has he not bought some Prebend?
Leandro’s money, makes the Rascall merry,
Merry at heart; he spies us.

sp.speaker: Lo
sp.ab:
Be gon Neighbours,The Bar & Book ready on a Cross-hatched lines.
Here are some Gentlemen: be gone good Neighbours,
Be gone, and labour to redeeme my favour,
No more words, but be gon: these two are Gnetlemen,
No company for crusty-handed fellowes.

sp.speaker: Dieg
sp.ab: We will stay for a yeare or two, and trie ye:

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
Fill all your hearts with joy, we will stay with ye,
Be gone, no more; I take your pastimes graciously:
Would ye with me (my friends?)

sp.speaker: Ars
sp.ab:
We would looke upon ye,
For me-thinks ye looke lovely.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
Ye have no Letters?
Nor any kind of Remembrances?

sp.speaker: Mil
sp.ab: Remembrances?

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
From Nova Hispania, or some part remote (Sir)
You looke like travell’d men: may be some old friends
That happily I have forgot; some Signeours
In China or Cataya; some Companions—

sp.speaker: Dieg
sp.ab: In the Mogulls Court, or else-where.

sp.speaker: Ars
sp.ab: They are mad sure.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
Ye came not from Peru? doe they look (Diego)
As if they had some mistery about em?
Another Don Alonzo now?

sp.speaker: Di
sp.ab:
I marry,
And so much money, Sir, from one you know not,
Let it be who it will.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
They have gracious favours.
Would ye be private?

sp.speaker: Mil
sp.ab:
There’s no need on’t (Sir)
We come to bring ye a Remembrance from a Merchant.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab: ’Tis very well, ’tis like I know him.

sp.speaker: Ars
sp.ab:
No, sir,
I doe not thinke ye doe.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
A new mistake (Diego)
Let’s carry it decently.

sp.speaker: Ars
sp.ab:
We come to tell ye,
You have received great summes from a young Factor
They call Leandro, that has rob’d his Master,
Rob’d him, and run away.

sp.speaker: Dieg
sp.ab:
Let’s keep close ( Master)
This newes comes from a cold Country.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab: By my faith it freezes,

sp.speaker: Mil
sp.ab: Curate)

sp.speaker: Mil
sp.ab:
Is not this true? doe you shrink now (good man
Doe I not touch ye?

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
We have a hundred Duckets
Yet left, we doe beseech ye sir—octa: Jacin & Ascanio be ready

sp.speaker: Mil
sp.ab: You’ll hang both.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab: One may suffice.

sp.speaker: Di
sp.ab:
I will not hang alone ( Master)
I had the least part, you shall hang the highest,
Plague o’ this Tiveria, and the Letter The
36
The divell sent it, post, to pepper us,
From Nova Hispania we shall hang at home now.

sp.speaker: Ars
sp.ab:
I see ye are penitent, and I have compas sion:
Ye are secure both; doe but what we charge ye,
Ye shall have more gold too, and he shall give it,
Ye ne’re indanger ye.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
Command us (Master)
Command us presently, and see how nimbly—

sp.speaker: Die
sp.ab: And if we doe not handsomely endeavour—

sp.speaker: Ars
sp.ab:
Goe home and till ye heare more keep private,
Till we appeare againe, no words, (Vicar)
There’s something added.

sp.speaker: Mil
sp.ab: For you too.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab: We are ready.

sp.speaker: Mil
sp.ab:
Goe, and expect us hourely, if ye falter,
Though ye had twenty lives—

sp.speaker: Die
sp.ab: We are fit to loose ’em.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab: ’Tis most expedient that we should hang both.

sp.speaker: Die
sp.ab: If we be hang’d, we cannot blame our fortune.

sp.speaker: Mil
sp.ab: Farewell, and be your owne friends.

sp.speaker: Lop,
sp.ab: We expect ye.—

sp.speaker: Oct
sp.ab: We cited to the Court!

sp.speaker: Ja
sp.ab: It is my wonder,

sp.speaker: Oct
sp.ab:
But not our fear, (Iacintha) wealthy men,(set out.
That have Estates to loose, whose conscious thoughts
Are full of inward guilt, may shake with horrour,
To have their Actions sifted, or appeareJamy & bar: be ready
Before the Judge. But we that know our selves
As innocent, as poore, that have no Fleece
On which the Talons of the griping Law
Can take sure hold, may smile with scorne on all
That can be urg’d against us.

sp.speaker: Ia
sp.ab:
I am confident
There is no man so covetous, that desires
To ravish our wants from us, and les se hope
There can be so much Justice left on earth,
(Though sude, and call’d upon) to ease us of
The burthen of our wrongs.

sp.speaker: Oct
sp.ab:
What thinkes Ascanio?
Should we be call’d in question or accus’d
Unjustly, what would you doe to redeeme us,
From tirannous oppres sion?

sp.speaker: Asc
sp.ab:
I could pray
To him that ever has an open eare
To heare the innocent, and right their wrongs;
Nay, by my tr[ ]th, I thinke I could plead
An Advocate, and sweat as much as he
Do’s for a double Fee, ere you should suffer
In an honest cause.

sp.speaker: Oct
sp.ab: Happy simplicitie!

sp.speaker: Ia
sp.ab: My dearest, and my best one: Don Iaime,

sp.speaker: Oct
sp.ab: And the Advocate, that caus’d us to be summond.

sp.speaker: Asc
sp.ab:
My Lord is mov’d, I see it in his lookes,
And that man, in the Gowne, in my opinion
Lookes like a proaguing knave.

sp.speaker: Iac
sp.ab: Peace, give them leave.

sp.speaker: Iam
sp.ab: Serve me with Proces se?

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab: My Lord, you are not lawles se.

sp.speaker: Iam
sp.ab:
Nor thou honest;
One, that not long since was the buckram Scribe,
That would run on mens errands for an Asper,
And from such basenes se, having rais’d a Stock
To bribe the covetous Judge call’d to the Bar,
So poore in practise too, that you would plead
A needy Clyents Cause, for a starv’d hen,
Or halfe a little loyn of Veale, though fly-blowne,
And these, the greatest Fees you could arrive at
For just proceedings; but since you turn’d Rascall—

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab: Good words, my Lord

sp.speaker: Iam
sp.ab:
And grew my Brothers Bawd
In all his vitious courses, soothing him
In his dishonest practises, you are growne
The rich, and eminent knave, in the divels name,
What am I cited for?

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
You shall know anon,
And then too late repent this bitter language,
Or I’ll mis se of my ends.

sp.speaker: Iam
sp.ab:
Wer’t not in Court,
I would beat that fat of thine, rais’d by the food
Snatch’d from poore Clyents mouthes, into a jelly:
I would (my man of Law) but I am patient,
And would obey the Judge.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
’Tis your best course:
Would every enemy I have would beat me,
I would wish no better Action.

sp.speaker: Oct
sp.ab: ’Save your Lordship.

sp.speaker: Asc
sp.ab: My humble service.

sp.speaker: Iam
sp.ab:
My good Boy, how dost thou?
Why art thou call’d into the Court?

div.stage: Enter As sistant, Henrique, Officer, and Witnes ses.

sp.speaker: Asc
sp.ab:
I know not,
But ’tis my Lord the As sistants pleasure
I should attend here.

sp.speaker: Iam
sp.ab: He will soone resolve us.

sp.speaker: Offic
sp.ab: Make way there for the Judge.

sp.speaker: Jam
sp.ab:
How? my kind Brother?
Nay then ’tis ranck: there is some villany towards.

sp.speaker: As sist
sp.ab:
’Tis Sessions purchas’d at your suit, Don Henrique,
Hath brought us hither, to heare and determine
Of what you can prefer.

sp.speaker: Henrique
sp.ab:
I doe beseech
The honourable Court, I may be heard
In my Advocate.

sp.speaker: As sist
sp.ab: ’Tis granted.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab: humh, humh.

sp.speaker: Jam
sp.ab:
That preface
If left out in a Lawyer, spoyles the Cause,
Though ne’re so good, and honest.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
If I stood here,
To plead in the defence of an ill man,
(Most equall Judge) or to accuse the innocent
(To both which, I profes se my selfe a stranger)
I would be requisite I should deck my Language
With Tropes and Figures, and all flourishes
That grace a Rethorician, ’tis confess’d
Adulterate Mettals, need the Gold-smiths Art,
To set ’em off; what, in it selfe is perfect
Contemnes a borrowed glos se: This Lord (my Client)
Whose honest cause, when ’tis related truly,
Will challenge Justice, finding in his conscience
A tender scruple of a fault long since
By him committed, thinkes it not sufficent
To be absolv’d of’t, by his Confes sor,
If that in open Court, he publish not
What so long conceal’d.

sp.speaker: Iam
sp.ab: To what tends this?

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
In his young yeares (it is no miracle
That youth, and heat of Blood, should mix together)
He look’d upon this woman, on whose face
The ruines yet remaine, of excellent forme,
He look’d on her, and lov’d her.

sp.speaker: Iac
sp.ab:
You good Angels,
What an imprudence is this?

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
And us’d all meanes
Of Service, Courtship, Presents, that might win her
To be at his devotion: but in vaine
Her maiden Fort, impregnable held out
Untill he promis’d Marriage; and before
These Witnes ses a solemne Contract pass’d
To take her as his wife.

sp.speaker: As sist
sp.ab: Give them their oath.
(tures,

sp.speaker: Iam
sp.ab:
They are incompetent Witnes ses, his own Crea-
And will sweare any thing for halfe a royall.

sp.speaker: Off
sp.ab: Silence.

sp.speaker: Assist
sp.ab: Proceed.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
Upon this strong assurance
He did enjoy his wishes to the full,
Which satisfied, and then with eyes of Judgement
(Had winck’d with lust before) considering duly
The inequality of the Match, he being
Nobly descended, and allyed, but she
Without a name, or Family, secretly
He purchas’d a Divorce, to disanull
His former Contract, marrying openly
The LadyViolante.

sp.speaker: Iac
sp.ab:
As you sit here
The Deputy of the great King, who is
The Substitute of that impartiall Judge
With whom, or Wealth, or titles prevaile nothing,
Grant to a much wrong’d Widow, or a Wife
Your patience, with liberty to speake
In her owne Cause, and let me face to face
To this bad man, deliver what he is:
And if my wrongs, with his ingratitude ballanc’d,
Move not compas sion, let me die unpittied;
His teares, his oathes, his perjuries, I pas se o’re
To thinke of them, is a disease; but death
Should I repeat them. I dare not deny,
(For Innocence cannot justifie what’s false)
But all the Advocate hath alleadged concerning
His falsehod, and my shame in my consent,
To be most true: But now I turne to thee,
To thee Don Henrique, and if impious Acts
Have left thee blood enough to make a blush,
I’ll paint it on thy cheekes. Was not the wrong
Sufficient to defeat me of mine honour,
To leave me full of sorrow, as of want,
The witnes se of thy lust, left in my womb,
To testifie thy falsehood, and my shame?
But now so many yeares I have conceal’d
Thy most inhumane wickednesse, and won
This Gentleman, to hide it from the world
To Father what was thine (for yet by heaven,
Though in the City, he pas’d for my husband,
He never knew me as his wife,)

sp.speaker: Assist
sp.ab:
’Tis strange:
Give him an Oath.

sp.speaker: Oct
sp.ab: I gladly sweare, and truly.

sp.speaker: Iac
sp.ab:
After all this (I say) when I had borne
These wrongs, with Saint-like patience, saw another
Freely enjoy, what was (in Justice) mine,
Yet still so tender of thy rest, and quiet,
I never would divulge it, to disturb
Thy peace at home, yet thou most barbarous,
To be so careles se of me, and my Fame,
(For all respect of thine in the first stepLines.
To thy base lust, was lost) in open Court Ches s-boord and
To publish my disgrace? and on record, men set ready.
To write me up an easie-yeilding wanton?
I thinke can find no president: In my extreames,
One comfort yet is left, that though the Law
Divorce me from thy bed, and made free way
To the unjust embraces of an other,
It cannot yet deny that this is thy Son
(Looke up Ascanio since it is come out)
Is thy legitimate heire.

sp.speaker: Iam
sp.ab:
Confederacie:
A trick (my Lord) to cheat me; e’re you give
Your sentence grant me hearing.

sp.speaker: Assist
sp.ab: New Chymera’s?

sp.speaker: Iam
sp.ab:
I am (my Lord) since he is without Is sue,
Or hope of any, his undoubted Heire,
And this forg’d by the Advocate, to defeat me
Of what the Lawes of Spaine confer upon me,
A meere Imposture, and conspiracie
Against my future fortunes,

sp.speaker: Assist
sp.ab:
You are too bold,
Speak to the Cause DonHenrique.

sp.speaker: Hen
sp.ab:
I confes se,
(Thou the acknowledgement must wound mine ho
nour,
That all the Court hath heard touching this Cause,
Or with me, or against me) is most true:
The later part my Brother urg’d, expected:
For what I now doe, is not out of Spleene
(As he pretends) but from remorse of conscience)
And to repaire the wrong that I have done
To this poore woman: And I beseech your Lordship
To thinke I have not so far lost my reason,
To bring into my Familie, to succeed me,
The stranger––Is sue of anothers Bed,
By proofe, this is my Son, I challenge him,
Accept him, and acknowledge him, and desire
By a definitive Sentence of the Court,
He may be so recorded, and full powre
To me, to take him home.

sp.speaker: Iac
sp.ab:
A second rape
To the poore remnant of Content, that’s left me,
If this be granted: and all my former wrongs
Were but beginnings to my miseries,
But this the height of all: rather then part
With my Ascanio, I’ll deny my oath,
Profes se my selfe a Strumpet, and endure
What punishment soe’re the Court decrees
Against a wretch that hath forsworne her selfe,
Or plai’d the impudent whore.

sp.speaker: Assist
sp.ab:
This tastes of passion,
And that must not divert the course of Justice;
Don Henrique, take your Son, with this Condition
You give him maintenance, as becomes his birth,
And ’twill stand with your honour to doe something
For this wronged woman: I will compell nothing,
But leave it to your will. Break up the Court:
It is in vaine to move me; my doom’s pass’d,
And cannot be revok’d. —

sp.speaker: Hen
sp.ab: There’s your reward.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
More Causes: and such Fees. Now to my Wife,
I have too long bin absent: Health to your Lordship,

sp.speaker: Asc
sp.ab:
You all look strangely, and I feare beleeve
This unexpected fortune makes me proud,
Indeed it do’s not: I shall ever pay you
The duty of a son, and honour you
Next to my Father: good my Lord, for yet
I dare not call you uncle, be not sad,
I never shall forget those noble favours
You did me being a stranger, and if ever
I live to be the master of a fortune,Bar: be ready.
You shall command it.

sp.speaker: Jam
sp.ab:
Since it was determi’nd
I should be cozen’d, I am, glad the profit
Shall fall on thee, I am too tough to melt,
But something will do.

sp.speaker: Hen
sp.ab:
’Pray you take leave
Of your steward (gentle Brother) the good husband
That takes up all for you.

sp.speaker: Jam
sp.ab:
Very well, mock on,
It is your turn: I may have mine—

sp.speaker: Oct
sp.ab:
But do not
Forget us deare Ascanio

sp.speaker: Asc
sp.ab:
Do not feare it,
I Every day will see you: every houre
Remember you in my prayers.

sp.speaker: Jam
sp.ab:
My grief’s too great
To be expres sed in words — —

sp.speaker: Hen
sp.ab:
Take that and leave us,
Leave us without reply, nay come back sirrah
And study to forget such things as these
As are not worth the knowledge.

sp.speaker: Asc
sp.ab:
O good Sir.
These are bad principles—

sp.speaker: Hen
sp.ab:
Such as you must learn
Now you are mine, for wealth and poverty
Can hold no friendship: and what is my will
You must observe and do, though good or ill.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
Where is my wife? ’fore heaven, I have done won
Done mighty things to day, my Amaranta,
My heart rejoyces at my wealthy Gleanings,
A rich litigious Lord I love to follow,
A Lord that builds his happines se on brawlings,
O ’tis a bles sed thing to have rich Clyents,
Why, wife I say, how fares my studious Pupill?
Hard at it still? ye are too violent
All things must have their rests, they will not last els
Come out and breathe.Cross-hatched lines.

sp.speaker: Lean
sp.ab:
I do beseech you pardon me
I am deeply in a sweet point Sir,

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
I’le instruct ye: Enter Amaranta. Cross-hatched lines.
I say take breath, seek health first, then your study,
O my sweet soul I have brought thee golden birds home
Birds in abundance. I have done strange wonders:
There’s more a hatching too.

sp.speaker: Am
sp.ab:
Have ye done good husband?
Then ’tis a good day spent

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
Good enough chicken,
I have spred the nets o’th’law,to catch rich booties,
And they come flttering in: how do’s my Pupil?
My modest thing, hast thou yet spoken to him?

sp.speaker: Am
sp.ab:
Am I past by his chamber I might see him,Moore with a chese bord
But he is so bookish,

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
And so bashfull too,
I faith he is, before he will speak, he will starve there

sp.speaker: Am
sp.ab: I pitie him a little.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab: So do I too.

sp.speaker: Am
sp.ab:
And if he please to take the aire o’th’ gardens
Or walk i’th’inward roomes, so he molest not—

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
He shall not trouble thee, he dare not speak to thee Enter Moore with Chesse-board
Bring out the Ches se-board,—come let’s have a game
wife,
I’le try your masterie, you say you are cunning

sp.speaker: Am
sp.ab: As learned as ye are (Sir) I shall beat ye

sp.speaker: Ba
sp.ab:
Here he steales out, put him not out of countenance
’Prethee look another way, he will be gone else
Walk and refresh your self, I’l be with you presently,

sp.speaker: Lean
sp.ab: I’le take the aire a little.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab: ’Twill be healthfnll.

sp.speaker: Am
sp.ab: Will ye be there? then here? Ile spare ye that man,

sp.speaker: Lean
sp.ab: ’Would I were so neare too, and a mate fitting.

sp.speaker: A
sp.ab: What thinke ye (, Sir) to this? have at your Knight now

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
’Twas subtilly playd: your Queen lies at my service
Pre thee look off, he is ready to pop in again
Look off I say, do’st thou not see how he blushes?

sp.speaker: Am
sp.ab: I do not blast him:moore be ready

sp.speaker: Lean
sp.ab:
You are a bles sed man that may so have her.Cross-hatched lines.
Oh that I might play with her—

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
Who’s there? I come, you cannot scape me now wife
I come, I come,

sp.speaker: Lean
sp.ab: Most bles sed hand that calls him.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab: Play quickly wife.

sp.speaker: Am
sp.ab: ’Pray ye give leave to think, Sir.

sp.speaker: Moore
sp.ab:
An honest neighbour that dwells hard by (Sir)
Would fain speak with your worship about busines se.

sp.speaker: Lean
sp.ab: The devil blow him off.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab: Play.

sp.speaker: Am
sp.ab:
I will study:
For if you beat me thus, you will still laugh at me—

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
He knocks again; I cannot stay. Leandro
’Pray thee come near.

sp.speaker: Lean
sp.ab: I am well (Sir) here,

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
Come hither:
Be not afraid but come.

sp.speaker: Am
sp.ab: Here’s none will bite (Sir)

sp.speaker: Lean
sp.ab: God forbid Lady.

sp.speaker: Am
sp.ab: ’Pray come nearer.

sp.speaker: Lean
sp.ab: Yes forsooth.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
’Pre thee observe these men: just as they stand here
And see this Lady, do not alter ’em,
And be not partiall, Pupill.

sp.speaker: Lean
sp.ab: No indeed Sir.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
Let her not move a pawn, I’le come back presently
Nay you shall know I am a Conquerour.
Have an eye Pupill——

sp.speaker: Am
sp.ab: Can ye play at Ches se Sir?

sp.speaker: Lean
sp.ab: A little Lady.

sp.speaker: Am
sp.ab:
But you cannot tell me
How to avoid this Mate, & win the Game too
Ha’s noble eyes: ye dare not friend me so farre.

sp.speaker: Lean
sp.ab:
I dare do any thing that’s in mans power, Lady, To
39
To be a friend to such a noble beauty.

sp.speaker: Am
sp.ab:
This is no Lawyers language: I pray ye tell me,
Whether may I remove, Ye see I am set round?
To avoid my husband.

sp.speaker: Lean
sp.ab:
I shall tell ye happily.
But happily you will not be instructed.

sp.speaker: Am
sp.ab: Yes, and I thank ye too, shall I move this man?

sp.speaker: Lean
sp.ab:
Those are unseemly: move one can serve ye
Can honour ye, can love ye.

sp.speaker: Am
sp.ab:
’Pray ye tell quickly
He will return and then

sp.speaker: Lean
sp.ab:
I’le tell ye instantly
Move me, and I wil move any way to serve ye
Move your heart this way ( Lady)

sp.speaker: Am
sp.ab: How?

sp.speaker: Lean
sp.ab:
’Pray ye heare me.
Behold the sport of Love, when he is imperious
Behold the slave of Love

sp.speaker: Am
sp.ab:
Move my Queen this way?bartolus be ready
Sure, he’s some worthy man: then if he hedge me
Or here to open him.

sp.speaker: Lean
sp.ab:
Do but behold me
If there be pity in you, do but view me,
But view the misery I have undertaken
For you the povertie.

sp.speaker: Am
sp.ab:
He will come presently.
Now play your best Sir, though I loose this Rook here
Yet I get Libertie.

sp.speaker: Lean
sp.ab:
I’le seize your fair hand
And warm it with a hundred, hundred kisses
The God of love warm your desires but equal
That shall play my game now.

sp.speaker: Am
sp.ab:
What do you mean Sir?
Why do you stop me?

sp.speaker: Lean
sp.ab:
That ye may intend me.
The time ha’s blest us both: Love bid us use it.
