I am a Gentleman nobly descended:
Young to invite your Love, rich to maintain it.
I bring a whole heart to ye, thus I give it,
And to those burning altars thus I offer,
And thus divine lips, where perpetuall Spring grows.

sp.speaker: Am
sp.ab: Take that, ye are too saucy.

sp.speaker: Lean
sp.ab:
How proud Lady?
Strike my deserts?

sp.speaker: Am
sp.ab: I was too blame.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
What wife, there?
Heaven keep my house from thieves.

sp.speaker: Lean
sp.ab:
I am wretched:
Opened, discovered, lost to my wishes.
I shall be whooted at.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
What noise was this (wife?)
Why dost thou ssile?

sp.speaker: Lean
sp.ab: This proud thing will betray me.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab: Why these lie here? what anger (deare?)

sp.speaker: Am,
sp.ab:
Why none, Sir,
Onely a chance your pupill said he plaid well,
And so indeed he do’s: he undertook for ye
Because I would not sit so long time idle
I made my Liberty, avoided your mate,
And he again as cunningly endangered me,
Indeed he put me strangely to it. When presently
Hearing you come, and having broke his ambush too
Having the second time brought off my Queen fair,
I rose o’th’ sudden smilingly to shew ye,
My apron caught the Ches se-board, and the men,
And there the noise was.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
Thou art grown a Master,Act
For all this, I shall beat ye.

sp.speaker: Lean
sp.ab:
Or I, Lawyer,
For now I love her more, ’twas a neat answer,
And it hangs by a mighty hope, I thank her
She gave my pate a sound knock that it rings yet,
But you shall have a sounder if I live Lawyer,
My heart akes yet I would not be in that fear—

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
I am glad ye are a ‘gamester, Sir, sometimes
For recreation we two shall fight hard at it,

sp.speaker: Am
sp.ab: He will prove too hard for me,

sp.speaker: Lean
sp.ab:
I hope he shall do,
But your Ches-board is too hard for my head, line that
good Lady,

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
I have been attoning, two most wrangling neig
bours,
They had no money, therefore I made even
Come, let’s go in, and eat, truly I am hungry.

sp.speaker: Lean
sp.ab: I have eaten already, I must intreat your pardon

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
Do as ye please, we shall expect ye at supper.
He ha’s got a little heart, not it seems handsomly,

sp.speaker: Am
sp.ab: You’l get no little head, if I do not look to ye.

sp.speaker: Lean
sp.ab: If ever I do catch thee again thou vanity—

sp.speaker: Am
sp.ab: I was too blame to be so rash, I am sorie—

sp.speaker: Hen
sp.ab: Heare but my reasons,

sp.speaker: Viol
sp.ab:
O my patience heare ’em.
Can cunning falshood colour an excuse?
With any seeming shape of borrowed truth?
Extenuate this wofull wrong, not error.

sp.speaker: Hen
sp.ab:
You gave consent that to defeat my brother
I should take any course,

sp.speaker: Viol
sp.ab:
But not to make
The cure more loathsome then the fowle disease:
Was’t not enough you took me to your bed,
Tir’d with loose dalliance, and with emptie veines,
All those abilities spent before and wasted,
That could conferre the name of mother on me?
But that (to perfect my account of sorrow)
For my long barrenes se you must highten it
By shewing to my face, that you were fruitfull
Hug’d in the base embraces of another?
If Solitude that dwelt beneath my roofe,
And want of children was a torment to me
What end my vexation to behold
A bastard to upbraid me with my wants?
And heare the name of father paid to ye
Yet know my self no mother,
What can I say?

sp.speaker: Hen
sp.ab:
shall I confesse my fault and ask your pardon?
Will that content ye?

sp.speaker: Viol
sp.ab:
If it could make void,
What is confirm’d in Court, No, no, Don Henrique,
You shall know that I find my self abus’d,
And adde to that I have a woman’s anger.
And while I look upon this Basilisk,
Whose envious eyes hath blasted all my comforts
Rest confident I’le study my dark ends,
And not your pleasures,

sp.speaker: Asc
sp.ab:
Noble Lady, heare me,
Not my Fathers son, but as your servant,
Vouchsafe to heare me, for such in my duty, I
40
I ever will appeare: And far be it from
My poore ambition, ever to looke on you,
But with that reverence; which a slave stands bound
To pay a worthy Mistris: I have heard
That Dames of highest place, nay Queenes themselves,
Disdaine not to be serv’d by such as are
Of meanest Birth: and I shall be most happie,
To be emploi’d when you please to command me
Even in the coursest Office, as your Page,
I can wayte on your trencher: : fill your wine
Carry your pontafles, and be sometimes bless’d
In all humilitie to touch your feete
Or if that you esteeme that too much grace
I can run by your Coach: observe your lookes
And hope to gaine a fortune by my service,
With your good favour, which now, as a Son,
I dare not challenge

sp.speaker: Viol
sp.ab: As a Son,

sp.speaker: Asc
sp.ab:
Forgive me
I will forget the name, let it be death
For me to call you Mother.

sp.speaker: Viol
sp.ab: Still upbraided?

sp.speaker: Hen
sp.ab: No way left to appease you?

sp.speaker: Viol
sp.ab:
None: now heare me:
Heare what I vow before the face of heaven,
And if I breake it all plagues in this life,
And those that after death are fear’d, fall on me
While that this Bastard staies under my rooffe,
Looke for no peace at home, for I renounce
All Offices of a wife,

sp.speaker: Hen
sp.ab: What am I falne to?

sp.speaker: Viol
sp.ab: (howers

sp.speaker: Viol
sp.ab:
I will not eate, nor sleepe with you and those
Which I should spend in prayers for your health
Shall be emploi’d in Curses,

sp.speaker: Hen
sp.ab: Terrible,

sp.speaker: Viol
sp.ab:
All the day long, i’le be as tedious to you
As lingring fevers, and i’le watch the nights,
To ring alou’d your shame, and breake your sleepes
Or if you doe but slumber, i’le appeare
In the shape of all my wrongs, and like a fury
Fright you to madnes, and if all this faile
To worke out my revenge, I have friends and kinsmen,
That will not sit downe tame with the disgrace
That’s offer’d to our noble familie
In what I suffer,

sp.speaker: Hen
sp.ab:
How am I devided
Betweene the duties I owe as a Husband,
And pietie of a Parent?

sp.speaker: Asc
sp.ab:
I am taught Sir
By the instinct of nature that obedience
Which bids me to prefer your peace of mind,
Before those pleasures that are dearest to me
Be wholy hers (my Lord) I quit all parts,
That I may challenge: may you grow old together
And no distast e’re find you and before
The Characters of age are printed on you
May you see many Images of your selves,
Though I, like some false Glasse, that’s never look’d in
Am cast a side, and broken from this hower
(Unles invited, which I dare not hope for)
I never will set my forbidden feete,
Over your threshold: onely give me leave
Though cast off to the world, to mention you,
In my devotions ’tis all I sue for
And so I take my last leave

sp.speaker: Hen
sp.ab:
Though I am
Devoted to a wife nay allmost sol’d
I slave to serve her pleasures, yet I cannot
So part with all humanity, but I must
Shew something of a Father: thou shalt not goe
Unfurnish’d and unfriended too: take that
To guard thee from neces sities; may thy goodnes
Deserve to be the heire of greater fortunes,
Then thou wer’t borne to. Scorne me not Violante
This banishment is a kind of civill death,
And now, as it were at his FunerallLe: Mil: ar:
To shed a teare or two, one word more,
And so farewell for ever: one word more,
Though I must never see thee (my Ascanio)
When this is spent (for so the Judge decreed)
Send to me for supply: are you pleas’d now?

sp.speaker: Viol
sp.ab:
Yes: I have cause: to see you howle and blubber
At the parting of my torment, & your shame Bed ready wine,
’Tis well, proceed; supply his wants: doe doe: table Standish &
Let the great dowre I brought serve to maintain Paper.
Your Bastards riots: send my Clothes and Jewells,
To your old acquaintance, your deare dame his Mother
Now you begin to melt, I know ’twill follow,

sp.speaker: Hen
sp.ab: Is all I doe misconstrude?

sp.speaker: Viol
sp.ab:
I will take
A course to right my self a speeding one:
By the bless’d Saints, I will; if I prove cruell
To shame to see thy foolish pitty, taught me
To loose my natural softness, keepe off from me
Thy flateries are infectious, and i’le fle thee
As I would doe a Leper.

sp.speaker: Hen
sp.ab:
Let not fury
Transport you so: you know I am your Creature.
All love, but to your self, with him, hath left me
I’le ioyne with you in any thing

sp.speaker: Viol
sp.ab:
In vaine
I’le take mine owne waies, and will have no partners,

sp.speaker: Hen
sp.ab: I will not cros se you,

sp.speaker: Viol
sp.ab:
Doe not, they shall find
That to a Woman of her hopes beguil’d
A viper troad on, or an Aspick’s mild.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
Sits the game there? I have you by mine order,
I love Leandro for’t

sp.speaker: Mil
sp.ab:
But you must shew it
In lending him your helpe, to gain him meane
And opportunitie.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
He shall want nothing,
I know my Advocate to a hayre, and what
Will fetch him from his prayers, if he use any,
I am honyed with the project: I would have him horn’d
For a most precious Beast.

sp.speaker: Ars
sp.ab: But you loose time;

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
I am gon, instruct you Diego, and you will find him
A sharpe and subtle knave, give him but hints
And he will amplifie: Se all things ready
I’ll fetch him with a vengeance.—

sp.speaker: Ars
sp.ab:
If ye faile now,
Wee’ll give him over too,

sp.speaker: Mil
sp.ab:
Tush he is flesh’d
And knowes what vaine to strike for his owne credit.

sp.speaker: Ars
sp.ab: All things are ready.

sp.speaker: Mil
sp.ab: Then we shall have a merry Scene, ne’re feare it.

div.stage: Enter Amaranta (with a note) and Moore.

sp.speaker: Amar
sp.ab: Is thy Master gone out?

sp.speaker: Moore
sp.ab:
Even now, the Curat fetc’h’d him,
About a serious businesss it seem’d,
For he snatch’d up his Cloack, and brush’d his hat strait,
Set his Band handsomely, and out he gallop’d.

sp.speaker: Amar
sp.ab:
’Tis wil, ’tis very well, he went out (Egla.)
As luckily, as one would say, goe Husband,
He was call’d by providence: fling this short paper
Into Leandro’s Cell, and waken him,
He is monstrous vexed, and musty, at my Ches se-play;
But this shall supple him, when he has read it:
Take your owne recreation for two houres,
And hinder nothing.

sp.speaker: Moore
sp.ab: If I doe, I’ll hang for’t.

sp.speaker: Oct
sp.ab:
If that you lov’d Ascanio for himselfe,
And not your private ends, you rather should
Bles se the faire opportunitie, that restores him
To his Birth-right, and the Honours he was borne to,
Then grieve at his good Fortune.Jam: & asca: be ready

sp.speaker: Jac
sp.ab:
Grieve Octavio?
I would resigne my Es sence, that he were
As happy as my love could fashion him,
Though every bles sing that should fall on him,
Might prove a curse to me, my sorrow springs
Out of my feare, and doubt he is not safe.
I am acquainted with Don Henrique’s nature,
And I have heard too much the fiery temper
Of Madam Violante: can you thinke
That she, that almost is at war with heaven
For being barren, will with equall eyes
Behold a Son of mine?

sp.speaker: Oct
sp.ab:
His Fathers care,
That for the want of Is sue, tooke him home,
(Though with the forfeiture of his own fame)
Will looke unto his safetie.

sp.speaker: Jac
sp.ab:
Step-mothers
Have many eyes, to find a way to mischiefe,
Though blind to goodnes se.

sp.speaker: Oct
sp.ab:
Here comes Don Jamy,
And with him our Ascanio.

sp.speaker: Jamy
sp.ab:
Good youth leave me,
I know thou art forbid my company,
And onely to be seene with me, will call on
Thy Fathers anger.

sp.speaker: Ars
sp.ab:
Sir, if that to serve you
Could loose me any thing (as indeed it cannot)
I still would follow you. Alas I was borne
To doe you hurt but not to help my selfe,
I was, for some particular end, tooke home,
But am cast off againe.

sp.speaker: Jam
sp.ab: Is’t pos sible?

sp.speaker: Asc
sp.ab:
The Lady, whom my Father calls his wife
Abhors my sight, is sick of me, and forc’d him
To turne me out of dores.

sp.speaker: Iac
sp.ab:
By my best hopes
I thanke her crueltie, for it comes neere
A saving charitie.

sp.speaker: Asc
sp.ab:
I am onely happy
That yet I can relieve you, ’pray you share
My Father’s wondrous kind, and promises
That I should be supplide: but sure the Lady
Is a malitious woman, and I feare
Meanes me no good.

sp.speaker: Iamy
sp.ab:
I am turn’d a stone with wonder,
And know not what to thinke.Lopez bartolus be ready

sp.speaker: Ser
sp.ab:
From my Lady,
Your private eare and this—

sp.speaker: Iamy
sp.ab: New Miracles?

sp.speaker: Ser
sp.ab:
She sayes, if you dare make your selfe a Fortune,
She will propose the meanes; My Lord Don Henrique
Is now from home and she alone expects you,
If you dare trust her so, if not despaire of
A second offer,

sp.speaker: Jam
sp.ab:
Though there were an Ambush
Layd for my life, I,ll on and sound this secret,
Retire thee (my Ascanio) with thy Mother:
But stir not forth, some great designe’s on foot,
Fall what can fall, if e’re the Sun be set,
I see you not give me dead.

sp.speaker: Asc
sp.ab:
We will expect you,
And those bless’d Angels, that love goodnes se, guard you.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab: Is’t pos sible he should be rich?

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
Most pos sible,
He hath bin long, though he has but little gettings,
Drawing together Sir.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
Accounted a poore Sexton,
Honest poore Diego,

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
I as sure ye, a close Fellow,
Both close, and scraping, and that fills the bags, Sir,

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab: A notable good Fellow too?Cross-hatched lines.

sp.speaker: Lopez
sp.ab:
Sometimes, Sir, Diego ready in Bed, wine, cup.
When he hop’d to drink a man into a surfeit,
That he might gaine by his Grave.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab: So many thousands?

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab: Heaven knowes what.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
’Tis strange,
,Tis very strange; but we see by endeavour,
And honest labour—

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
Milo by continuance
Grew from a silly Calfe (with your worships reverence)
To carry a Bull from a penny, to a pound, Sir,
And from a pound, to many: ’tis the progres se.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
Ye say true, but he lov’d to feed well also,
And that me-thinks—

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
From another mans Trencher, Sir,
And there he found it season’d with small charge:
There he would play the Tyrant, and would devoure ye
More then the Graves he made at home he liv’d
Like a Camelion, suckt th’Ayre of misery, Table out Stan-
And grew fat by th’Brewis of an Eg-shel, dish paper, stools. Would
42 [...]asenio & parishioners
Would smell a Cooks shop, and goe home and surfeit,
And be a moneth in fasting out that Fever.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab: (ye?

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
These are very good Symptomes: do’s he lye so sick, say
(ye?

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
Oh, very
good Lady,ick.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab: And chosen me Executor?

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab: Onely one Worship.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab: No hope of his amendment?

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab: None, that we find.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab: He hath no kinsmen neither?

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab: ’Truth, very few.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
His mind will be the quieter,
What Doctors has he?

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab: There’s none sir, he believes in.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
They are but needles se things, in such exteremities.
Who drawes the good-man’s will?

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
Marry that doe I, Sir.
And to my griefe.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
Griefe will doe little now, Sir,
Draw it to your comfort, Friend, and as I counsell ye,
An honest man, but such men live not alwayes
Who are about him?

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
Many now he is pas sing,
That would pretend to his love, yes, and some gentlemen
That would faine counsell him, and be of his kindred;
Rich men can want no heires, Sir.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
They doe ill,
Indeed they doe, to trouble him: very ill, Sir,
But we shall take a care.Cross-hatched lines.

div.stage: Enter Diego (in a bed) Millanes, Arsenio, and Parishioners.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
Will ye come neare, Sir,
’Pray ye bring him out; Now ye may see in what state:
Give him fresh ayre.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
I am sorry Neighbour Diego,
To find ye in so weake a state.

sp.speaker: Die
sp.ab:
Ye are welcome,
But I am fleeting, Sir.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
Me-thinkes he looks well,
His colour fresh, and strong, his eyes are chearfull.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
A glimmering before death ’tis nothing els, Sir,
Do you see how he fumbles with the sheet? do ye note that

sp.speaker: Di
sp.ab:
My learned Sir ’pray ye sit: I am bold to send for ye,
To take care of what I leave.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab: Doe you heare that?

sp.speaker: Ars
sp.ab: Play the knave finely.

sp.speaker: Die
sp.ab:
So I will, I warrant ye,
And carefully.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
’Pray ye doe not trouble him,
You see he’s weake and has a wandring fancie.

sp.speaker: Di
sp.ab:
My honest Neighbours, weep not, I must leave ye,
I cannot alwayes beare ye company,
VVe must drop still there is no remedie:
’Pray ye Master Curat, will ye write my Testament,
And write it largely it may be remembered
And be witnes se to my Legacies good Gentlemen;
Your worship I doe make my full Executor,
You are a man of wit and understanding:
Give me a cup of wine to raise my Spirits,
For I speake low: I would before these Neighbours
Have ye to sweare (Sir) that you will see it executed,
And what I give, let equally be rendered
For my soules health.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
I vow it truly, Neighbours,
Let not that trouble ye before all these
Once more I give my Oath.

sp.speaker: Di
sp.ab:
Then set me higher,
And pray ye come neare me all.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab: VVe are ready for ye.

sp.speaker: Mil
sp.ab: Now spur the As se, and get our friend time.

sp.speaker: Die
sp.ab:
First then,
After I have given my Body to the wormes
(For they must be serv’d first, they are seldome cozen’d)

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab: Remember your Parish, Neighbour.

sp.speaker: Di
sp.ab:
You speake truly,
I doe remember it, a lewd vile Parish,
And pray it may be mended: To the Poore of it,
(VVhich is to all the Parish) I give nothing,
For nothing, unto nothing, is most naturall,
Yet leave as much space, as will build a Hospitall,
Their children may pray for me.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab: What doe you give to it?

sp.speaker: Die
sp.ab: Set downe two thousand Duckets,

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
’Tis a good gift,
And will be long remembered.

sp.speaker: Die
sp.ab:
To your worship,
(Because you must take paines to see all finish’d)
I give two thousand more, it may be three, Sir,
A poore gratuitie for your paines-taking.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab: These are large summes;

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab: Nothing to him that has ’em.

sp.speaker: Die
sp.ab:
To my old Master Vicar I give five hundred,
(Five hundred, and five hundred, are too few Sir)
But there be more to serve.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab: This fellow coynes sure.

sp.speaker: Di
sp.ab:
Give me some more drink. Pray ye buy Books, buy
Books,
You have a learned head stuffe it with Libraries,
And understand ’em, when you have done, ’tis Justice,
Run not the Parish mad with Controversies,
Nor preach not Abstinence to longing women,
’Twill budge the bottoms of their consciences:
I would give the Church new Organs, but I prophecie
The Church-wardens would quickly pipe’em out o’the’Pa
rish,-
Two hundred Duckets more to mend the chancel,
And to paint true Orthographie, as many,
They write Sunt with a C which is abominable,
’Pray you set that downe, to poore Maidens marriages.

sp.speaker: Lo
sp.ab:
I that’s wel thought of, what’s your wil in that point?
A meritorious thing.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab: No end of this will?

sp.speaker: Di
sp.ab:
I give per annum two hundred ells of Lockram,
That there be no strait dealings in their Linnens,
But the Sayles cut according to their Burthens;
To all Bell-Ringers, I bequeath new Ropes,
And let them use ’em at their owne discretions.

sp.speaker: Ars
sp.ab: You may remember us.

sp.speaker: Di
sp.ab:
I doe, good Gentlemen,
And I bequeath ye both good carefull Surgeons
A Legacy, you have need of, more then money,
I know you want good Diets and good Lotions,
And in your pleasures good take heed.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
He raves now.
But ’twill be quickly off,

sp.speaker: Di
sp.ab:
I doe bequeath ye
Commodities of pins: browne papers: pack-threds,
Rost proke, & puddings: Ginger-bread, & Jewes-trumps;
Of penny Pipes, and mouldy Pepper: take ’em,
Take ’em even where you please and be cozen’d with ’em,
I should bequeath ye Executions also,
But those I’ll leave to th’Law.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab: Now he growes temperate.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab: You will give no more?

sp.speaker: Di
sp.ab:
I am loth to give more from ye, Because
G2 43
Because I know you will have a care to execute
Onely, to pious uses, Sir, a little.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab: If he be worth all these, I am made for ever,

sp.speaker: Die
sp.ab:
I give to fatall Dames, that spin mens threds out,
And poore distres sed Damsells, that are militant
As members of our owne Afflictions,
A hundred Crowns to buy warm tubbs to worke in,
I give five hundred pounds to buy a Church-yard,
A spacious Church-yard, to lay Theeves and knaves in,
Rich men, and honest men, take all the roome up.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab: Are ye not weary?

sp.speaker: Di
sp.ab: Never of well-doing.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab: These are mad Legacies.

sp.speaker: Die
Bar
sp.ab: This cannot be, ’tis Monstrous.

sp.speaker: Die
sp.ab: Three Ships at Sea too.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab: You have made me full Executor.

sp.speaker: Di
sp.ab:
Full, full, and totall, would I had more to give ye
But these may serve an honest mind.

sp.speaker: Bar
Die
sp.ab:
Even where you please Sir,
You are wise and provident, and know busines se
Ev’n raise ’em where you shal think good, I am reasonable

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
Thinke good? will that raise thousands?
What doe you make me?

sp.speaker: Di
sp.ab: You have sworn to see it done, that’s all my comfort.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab: Where I please? this is pack’d sure to disgrace me.

sp.speaker: Di
sp.ab:
You are just, and honest, and I know you will doe it,
Ev’n where you please, for you know where the wealth is.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
I am abused, betrayed, I am laugh’d at, scorn’d,
Baffel’d, and boared, it seemes.

sp.speaker: Ars
sp.ab: No, no, ye are fooled.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
Most finely fooled, and handsomely, and neatly,
Such cunning Masters must be fooled sometimes, Sir,
And have their worships noses wiped, ’tis healthfull,
We are but quit: you foole us of our moneys
In every Cause, in every Quiddit wipe us.

sp.speaker: Di
sp.ab:
Ha, ha, ha, ha, some more drink, for my heart, Gentle
men
This merry Lawyer—ha,ha,ha,ha, this Scholler—
I thinke this fitt will cure me: this Executor—
I shall laugh out my Lungs.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
This is derision above sufferance, villany
Plotted, and set against me.

sp.speaker: Die
sp.ab:
Faith ’tis knavery,
In troth I must confes se, thou art fooled indeed, Lawyer.

sp.speaker: Mil
sp.ab: Did you thinke, had this man been rich—

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab: ’Tis well, Sir.

sp.speaker: Mil
sp.ab:
He would have chosen such a Wolfe, a Cancker,
A Maggot-pate, to be his whole Executor.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
A Lawyer, that entangles all mens honesties,
And lives like a Spider in a Cobweb lurking,
And catching at all Flies, that pas se his pitt-falls?
Puts powder to all States, to make ’em caper?
Would he trust you?

sp.speaker: Die
sp.ab:
Doe you deserve? I find, Gentlemen,
This Cataplasme of a well cozen’d Lawyer
Laid to my stomach lenifies my Fever,
Me-thinkes I could eat now and walke a little.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
I am asham’d to feele how flat I am cheated,
How gros sely, and malitiously made a May-game,
A damned Trick; my wife, my wife, some Rascall:
My credit, and my wife, some lustfull villaine,
Some Bawd, some Rogue,Amararan & Leandro be ready

sp.speaker: Ars
sp.ab:
Some craftie Foole has found ye:
This ’tis Sir, to teach ye to be too busie,
To covet all the gaines, and all the rumours.
To have a stirring oare, in all mens actions.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab: We did this, but to vex your fine officiousnes se.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
Good yeild ye and go’d thank ye: I am fooled, gen
(tlemen;-
The Lawyer is an As se, I doe confes se it,
A weak dull shallow As se: good even to your worships:
Vicar, remember Vicar, Rascall remember,
Thou notable rich Rascall.

sp.speaker: Die
sp.ab:
I doe remember, Sir,
’Pray ye stay a little, I have ev’n two Legacies
To make your mouth up, sir.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
Remember Varletts,
Quake & remember, Rouges; I have brine for your But
tocks. Ex.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab: Oh how he frets, and fumes now like a dunghill.

sp.speaker: Di
sp.ab:
His gall containes fine stuffe now to make poysons,
Rare damned stuffe.

sp.speaker: Ars
sp.ab:
Let’s after him, and still vex him,
And take my Friend off: by this time he has prosper’d,
He cannot loose this deere time: ’tis impos sible.

sp.speaker: Mil
sp.ab: Well Diego, thou hast done.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab: Hast done it daintily.

sp.speaker: Mil
sp.ab: And shalt be as well paid, Boy—

sp.speaker: Ars
sp.ab: Goe, let’s crucifie him.

sp.speaker: Lea
sp.ab: I have told ye all my story, and how desperately.

sp.speaker: Am
sp.ab:
I doe believe: let’s walke on, time is pretious,
Not to be spent in words, here no more wooing,
The open Ayre’s an enemy to Lovers, Pewter ready
Doe as I tell ye. for noyse.

sp.speaker: Lea
sp.ab:
I’ll doe any thing,Cross-hatched lines.
I am so over-joy’d, I’ll fly to serve ye.

sp.speaker: Am
sp.ab:
Take your joy moderately, as it is ministred,
And as the cause invites: that man’s a foolebartolus be ready
That at the sight o’th’Bond, dances and leapes,
Then is the true joy, when the money comes.

sp.speaker: Lea
sp.ab: You cannot now deny me.

sp.speaker: >Am
sp.ab:
Nay, you know not,
Women have crotchets, and strange fits.

sp.speaker: Lea
sp.ab: You shall not.

sp.speaker: Am
sp.ab:
Hold ye to that and sweare it confidently,
Then I shall make a scruple to deny ye:
’Pray ye let’s step in, and see a friend of mine,
The weather’s sharp: we’ll stay but halfe an houre,
We may be miss’d els: a private fine house ’tis, Sir,
And we may find many good welcomes.

sp.speaker: Lea
sp.ab:
Doe Lady,
Doe happy Lady.

sp.speaker: Am
sp.ab:
All your mind’s of doing,
You must be modester.

sp.speaker: Lea
sp.ab: I will be any thing.—

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
Open the dores, and give me roome to chafe in
Mine owne romme, and my liberty: why Maid there, Open
44 lo: Ar: Mill: Diego be ready
Open, I say, and doe not anger me,
I am subject to much fury: when ye dish-clout?
When doe ye come? a sleepe, ye lazie hell-hound?
Nothing intended, but your ease, and eating?
No body here? why wife, why wife? why jewell?
No tongue to answer me? ’pree’thee (good Pupill)
Dispence a little with thy careful study,
And step to th’ doore, and let me in; nor he neither?
Ha! not at’s study? nor asleepe? nor no-body?
I’ll make ye heare: the house of Ignorance,
No sound inhabitants here: I have a key yet
That commands all: I feare I am metamorphiz’d.Cross-hatched lines.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab: He keepes his fury still, and may doe mischiefe.

sp.speaker: Mil
sp.ab: He shalbe hang’d first, we’ll be sticklers there, boyes

sp.speaker: Di
sp.ab:
The hundred thousand Dreams now, that pos ses him
Of jealousie, and of revenge, and frailtie
Of drawing Bills against us, and Petitions.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab: And casting what his credit shall recover.

sp.speaker: Mil
sp.ab:
Let him cast till his Maw came up, we care not.
You shall be still secured.

sp.speaker: Die
sp.ab:
We’ll pay him home then;
Hark what a noyse he keeps within?

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
Certaine Cross-hatched lines.
H’as set his Chimneys o’ fire, or the divell roars there.

sp.speaker: Di
sp.ab: The Codixes o’th’ Law are broke loose,

sp.speaker: Ars
sp.ab: He’s fighting sure,

sp.speaker: Di
sp.ab: I’ll tell ye that immediatly—.

sp.speaker: Mil
sp.ab: Or doing some strange out-rage on himselfe.

sp.speaker: Ars
sp.ab: Hang him, he dares not be so valiant.

sp.speaker: Di
sp.ab:
There’s no body at home and he chases like a Lyon, Ama Leandro be ready
And stinkes withall.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab: No body?

sp.speaker: Di
sp.ab:
Not a creature,
Nothing within, but he and his Law-tempest,
The Ladles, dishes, kettles, how they fly all?
And how the Glas ses through the Roomes?

sp.speaker: Ars
sp.ab:
My friends sure
Has got her out, and now he has made an end on’t.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
See where the Sea comes? how it foams & brus sels?
The great Leviathan o’th’ Law, how it tumbles?

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
Made every way an As se? abus’d on all sides?
And from all quarters. people come to laugh at me?
Rise like a Comet, to be wonder’d at?
A horrid Comet, for Boyes tongues, and Ballads?
I will run from my wits.

sp.speaker: Ars
sp.ab:
Doe, doe (good Lawyer)
And from thy money too, then thou wilt be quiet.

sp.speaker: Mil
Ars
sp.ab: She has pull’d his eares downe.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
Now, what sweet voyage? to what Garden, Lady?
Or to what Cosens house?

sp.speaker: Am
sp.ab:
Is this my welcome?
I cannot goe to Church, but thus I am scandall’d,
Use no devotion for my soule, but Gentlemen—

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab: To Church?

sp.speaker: Am
sp.ab:
Yes, and ye keep sweet youths to wait upon me,
Sweet bred-up youths, to be a credit to me.
There’s your delight againe, pray take him to ye,
He never comes neare me more to debase me.

sp.speaker: Ba
sp.ab:
How’s this? how’s this? good wife, how has he wrongd
ye?

sp.speaker: Am
sp.ab:
I am faine to drive him like a sheep before me,
I blush to thinke how people fleere, and scorn’d me,
Others have handsome men, that know behaviour,
Place, and observance: this silly thing knowes nothing,
Cannot tell ten; Let every Rascall justle me,
And still I push’d him on, as he had bin comming.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab: Ha! did ye push him on? is he so stupid?

sp.speaker: Am
sp.ab:
When others were attentive to the Priest,
Good devout Gentleman, then fell he fast
Fast, sound asleep: then first began the Bag-pipes
The severall stops on’s nose, made a rare musick,
A rare and lowd, and those plaid many an Antheme
Put out of that, he fell strait into dreaming.

sp.speaker: Ars
sp.ab: As cunning as she is sweet; I like this carriage.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab: What did he then?

sp.speaker: Am
sp.ab:
Why then he talked in his Sleep too,
Nay, I’ll divulge your morall vertues (sheeps-face)
And talk’d aloude, that every eare was fixt to him:
Did not I suffer (doe you thinke) in this time?
Talk of your bawling Law, of appellations
Of Declarations, and Excommunications:
Warrants, the Executions: and such divells
That drove all the Gentlemen out o’th’Church, by hur
ryes
With execrable oaths, they would never come there again
Thus am I serv’d, and man’d.

sp.speaker: Lea
sp.ab:
I pray ye forgive me,
I must confes se I am not fit to wait upon ye:
Alas, I was brought up—

sp.speaker: Am
sp.ab:
To be an As se,
A Lawyers As se, to carry Bookes, and Buckrams.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab: But what did you at Church?

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
At Church, did ye aske her?
Doe you heare gentlemen, doe you mark the question?
Because you are halfe an heretique your selfe, Sir,
Would ye breed her too? this shall to the Inquisition,
A pious Gentlewoman, reprov’d for praying?
I’ll see this filed, and you shall heare further, Sir.

sp.speaker: Ars
sp.ab: Ye have an ill heart.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
It shall be found out Gentlemen,
There be those youths will search it.

sp.speaker: Die
sp.ab:
You are warme Signiour,
But a Faggot will warme ye better: we are witnes ses.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab: Enough to hang him, doe not doubt.

sp.speaker: Mil
sp.ab:
Nay certaine,
I doe beleeve has rather no Religion.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab: (Church, sir?

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
That must be knowne too, because shee goes to
(Church sir?
O monstrum informe ingens!

sp.speaker: Die
sp.ab:
Let him goe on, sir,
His wealth will build a Nunnery, a faire one,
And this good Lady, when he is hang’d, and rotten,
May there be Abbes se.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
You are cozend, honest Gentlemen,
I doe not forbid the use, but the forme, marke me.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab: Forme? what doe ye make of Forme?

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
They will undoe me,
Sweare, as I oft have done, and so betray me;
I must make faire way, and hereafter, Wife,
You are welcome home, & henceforth take your pleasure,
Goe, when ye shall thinke fit, I will not hinder ye,
My eyes are open now, and I see my e[]rour,
My shame, as great as that, but I must hide it.
The whole conveyance now I smell, but Basta,
Another time must serve: you see us friends, now
Heartily friends, and no more chiding (gentlemen)
I have bin too foolish, I confes se, no more words,
No more (sweet wife.)

sp.speaker: Am
sp.ab: You know my easie nature

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
Goe get ye in: you see she has bin angry:
Forebeare her fight a while and time will pacify.
And learne to be more bold.

sp.speaker: Lea
sp.ab:
I would I could,
I will doe all I am able.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
Doe Leandro.Act
We will not part, but friends of all hands.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
Well said,
Now ye are reasonable, we can looke on ye,

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
Ye have ierckt me: but for all that I forgive ye
Forgive ye hartily, and doe invite ye
Tomorrow to a Breakfast, I make but seldome
But now we will be merry.

sp.speaker: Ars
sp.ab:
Now ye are friendly,
Your doggednes and nigardize flung from ye,
And now we will come to ye

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
Give me your hands, all;
You shall be wellcome hartily.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
We will be,
For wee’ll eate hard

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
The harder, the more wellcome,
And till the morning farewell; I have busines.

sp.speaker: Mil
sp.ab:
Farewell good bountiful Bartolus ’tis a brave wench
A sudaine witty Theif, and worth all service:
Goe wee’ll all goe, and crucifie the Lawyer,

sp.speaker: Die
sp.ab:
I’ll clap foure tire of teeth into my mouth more
But I will grind his substance.

sp.speaker: Ars
sp.ab:
Well Leandro,
Thou hast had a strange voyage, but I hope
Thou rid’st now in safe harbour,

sp.speaker: Mil
sp.ab:
Lets goe drinke, Friends,
And laugh alou’d at all our merry may-games

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab: A match, a match ’twill whet our stomachs better.

sp.speaker: Ser
sp.ab: Madam hees come.

sp.speaker: Viol
sp.ab:
Tis well how did he looke,
When he knew from whom you were sent? was he not
startled
Or confident? or fearfull?

sp.speaker: Ser
sp.ab:
As appear’d
Like one that knew his fortune at the worst,
And car’d not what could follow.

sp.speaker: Viol
sp.ab:
’Tis the better
Reach me a Chaire: So bring him in, be carefull
That none disturb us: I will try his temper,
And if I find him apt for my employments,

sp.speaker: Viol
sp.ab:
I’ll worke him to my ends, if not I shall
Find other Engines.

sp.speaker: Ser
sp.ab: Ther’s my Ladie,

sp.speaker: Viol
sp.ab: Leave us

sp.speaker: Iam
sp.ab: You sent for me?

sp.speaker: Viol
sp.ab:
I did, and do’s the favour,
Your present state considered, and my power,
Deserve no greater Ceremonie?

sp.speaker: Iam
sp.ab:
Ceremonie?
I use to pay that, where I doe owe dutie,
Not to my Brothers wife: I cannot fawne,
If you expect it from me, you are cozen’d,
And so farewell.

sp.speaker: Viol
sp.ab:
He beares up still; I like it,
Pray you a word

sp.speaker: Iam
sp.ab:
Yes: I will give you hearing
On equall termes, and sit by you as a friend,
But not stand as a Sutour: Now your pleasure?

sp.speaker: Viol
sp.ab: You are very bold.

sp.speaker: Iam
sp.ab:
’Tis fitt: since you are proud
I was not made to feed that foolish humour,
With flattery and observance

sp.speaker: Viol
sp.ab:
Yet, with your favour,
A little forme ioyn’d with respect to her,
That can add to your wants, or free you from ’em
(Nay raise you to a fate, beyond your hopes) A Table ready co-
Might well become your wisedome, vered with Cloath

sp.speaker: Iam
sp.ab:
It would rather Napkins Salt
Write me a Foole, should I but onely think Treachers and
That any good to me, could flow from you, Bread.
Whom for so many yeares: I have found and prov’d
My greatest Enemy: I am still the same
My wants have not transform’d me: I dare tell you,
To your new cerviz’d face, what I have spoken
Freely behind your back, what I thinke of you,
You are the proudest thing, and have the least,
Reason to be so, that I ever read of
In stature you are a Giantesse: and your Tailour
Takes measure of you, with a Iacobs staffe,
Or he can never reach you, this is by the way
For your large size: Now, in a word, or two
To treat of your Complexion were decorum:
You are so far from faire, I doubt your Mother
Was too familliar with the Moore, that serv’d her,
Your Limbes and Features, I pas se breifely over,
As things not worth description; and come roundly
To your soule, if you have any: for ’tis doubtfull

sp.speaker: Viol
sp.ab: I laugh at this, proceed

sp.speaker: Iam
sp.ab:
This Soule, I speake of
Or rather salt to keepe this heape of flesh,
From being a walking stench, like a large Inne,
Stands open for the entertainement of
A!l impious practices: but ther’s no Corner
An honest thought can take up: and as it were not
Sufficent in your self to comprehend
All wicked plots, you have taught the Foole, my Brother
By your contagion, almost to put off
The nature of the man, and turn’d him Devill
Because he should be like you, and I hope
Will march to hell together: I have spoken,
And if the limming you, in your true Colours
Can make the Painter gracious, I stand readie
For my reward, or if my words distaste you
I weigh it not, for though your Groomes were readie
To cut my throat for’t be as sur’d I cannot
Use other Language

sp.speaker: Viol
sp.ab:
You thinke you have said now,
Like a brave fellow: in this Womans War
You ever have bin train’d: spoke big: but suffer’d
Like a tame As se; and when most spur’d and gall’d
Were never Master of the Spleene or Spirit,
That could raise up the anger of a man,
And force it into action,

sp.speaker: Iam
sp.ab:
Yes vile Creature
Wer’t thou a subject worthy of my Sword,
Or that thy death, this moment, could call home,
My banish’d hopes, thou now wer’t dead: dead (woman)
But being as thou art it is sufficient
I scorne thee, and contemne thee

sp.speaker: Viol
sp.ab:
This shewes nobly: I
46
I must confes se it: I am taken with it
For you had kneeld, and whind and shew’d a base
And low deiected mind, I had despis’d you
This Bravery (in your adverse fortune) conquers
And do’s command me, and upon the sudaine
I feele a kind of pittie, growing in me,
For your misfortunes, pittie some sayes the Parent,
Of future love, and I repent my part,
So far in what you have suffered, that I could,
(But you are cold) doe something to repaire
What your base Brother (such Iami I thinke him)
Hath brought to ruine

sp.speaker: Iam
sp.ab: Ha?

sp.speaker: Viol
sp.ab:
Be not amaz’d,
Our injuries are equall in his Bastard
You are familliar with what I grone for
And though the name of Husband holds a tye
Beyond a Brother, I, a poore weake Woman,
Am sensible, and tender of a wrong,
And to revenge it, would break through all letts,
That durst oppose me.

sp.speaker: Iam
sp.ab: Is it pos sible?

sp.speaker: Viol
sp.ab:
By this kis se: start not: thus much, as a stranger
You may take from me; But, if you were pleas’d,
I should select you, as a bosome Friend,
I would print ’em, thus, and, thus,

sp.speaker: Iam
sp.ab: Keepe off.

sp.speaker: Viol
sp.ab:
Come neare,
Neere into the Cabinet of my Counsailes:
Simplicity and patience dwells with Fooles,
And let them beare those burthens, which wise men
Boldly shake off; Be mine and ioyne with me,
And when that I have rais’d you to a fortune,
(Doe not deny your selfe the happie meanes)
You’l looke on me, with more iudicious eies
And sweare I am most faire,

sp.speaker: Iam
sp.ab:
What would this Woman?
The purpose of these words? speake not in ridles
And when I understand, what you would counsell,
My answer shall be suddaine,

sp.speaker: Viol
sp.ab:
Thus then Iami,
The objects of our fury, are they same,
For young Ascanio, whom you snake like hug’d
(Frozen with wants to death) in your warme bosome,
Lives to supplant you in your certaine hopes,
And kills in me all comfort.

sp.speaker: Iam
sp.ab:
Now ’tis plaine,
I apprehend you: and were he remov’d—

sp.speaker: Viol
sp.ab: You, once againe, were the undoubted heire.

sp.speaker: Iam
sp.ab:
’Tis not to be denyed; I was ice before,
But now ye have fir’d me,—

sp.speaker: Viol
sp.ab:
I’l add fuell to it,
And by a nearer cut, doe you but steere
As I direct you bring our Bark into
The Port of happines,

sp.speaker: Iam
sp.ab: How?

sp.speaker: Viol
sp.ab:
By Henriques death:
But you’ll say hee’s your Brother; in great fortunes
(Which are epitomes of States & Kingdomes) Dishes cove-
The politicke brooke no Rivalls. red with pa-

sp.speaker: Iam
sp.ab:
Excellent. pers in each
For sure I thinke out of a scrupulous feare, ready.
To feed in expectation, when I may
(Dispensing but a little with my conscience)
Come into full pos ses sion, would not argue
One that desir’d to thrive,

sp.speaker: Viol
sp.ab:
Now you speake like
A man that knowes the World.

sp.speaker: Jam
sp.ab:
I needs must learne
That have so good a Tutres se: And what thinke you,
(Don Henrique and Ascanio cut off)
That none may live, that shall desire to trace us
In our black pathes, if that Octavio
His foster Father’ and the sad Jacinta,
(Faith pittie her, and free her from her Sorrowes)
Should fall Companions with ’em? When we are red
With murther, let us often bath in blood,
The collour will be scarlet.

sp.speaker: Viol
sp.ab:
And that’s glorious,be ready
And will protect the fact

sp.speaker: Jam
sp.ab:
Suppose this don:
(If undiscovered,) we may get for money,
(As that you know buyes any thing in Rome)
A dispensation

sp.speaker: Viol
sp.ab: And be married?

sp.speaker: Jam
sp.ab:
True.
Or if it be knowne, trus se up our Gold and Jewells,
And fly to some free State, and there with scorne—

sp.speaker: Viol
sp.ab:
Laugh at the lawes of Spaine.
’Twere admirable.

sp.speaker: Iam
sp.ab:
We shall beget rare Children. I am rap’d with
The meere imagination—

sp.speaker: Viol
sp.ab: Shall it be don?

sp.speaker: Iam
sp.ab:
Shall? tis too tedious: furnish me with meanes
To hire the instruments, and to your self,
Say it is done already: I will shew you,
’Ere the Sun set, how much you have wrought upon me,
Your province is onely to use some meanes,
To send my Brother, to the Grove that’s neighbour,
To the west Port of th’ Citie; leave the rest,
To my owne practice; I have talk’d too long.
But now will doe: this kis se, with my Confes sion,
To worke a fell revenge: A mans a foole,
If not instructed in a Womans Schoole.

div.stage: Enter Bartolus Algazier and a Paratour.
The Table set out and stooles.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
You are well enough disguiz’d, furnish the Table,
Make no shew, what ye are, till I discover
Not a soule knowes ye here: be quick and dilligent,
These youthes, I have invited to a Breakfast,
But what the Sawce will be, I am of opinion
I shall take off the edges of their Appetites,
And greaze their gums, for eating hartily;
This month of two they have plaid their prizes with me
And their severall flurts they have lighted dange-
But sure I shall be quit: I heare ߴem comming (rously
Goe off, and wait the bringing in your service,
And doe it handsomely: you know where to have it Enter Millanes, Arsenio, Lopez, Diego.
Wellcome i’Faith,

sp.speaker: Ars
sp.ab: That’s well said, honest Lawyer,

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab: Said like a Neighbour

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
Wellcome all: all over
And let’s be merry:

sp.speaker: Mil
sp.ab:
To that end we came Sir,
An hower of freedome’s worth an age of juglings,

sp.speaker: Die
sp.ab:
I am come too Sir, to specifie my Stomach
A poore reteyner to your worships bountie,

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
And thou shalt have it fill’d, my merry Diego,
My liberall, and my bonney bounteous Diego
Even filld till it groane againeAma: lean: be ready.

sp.speaker: Di
sp.ab:
Let it have faire play,
And if it founder then—
I’ll tell ye neighbours,
Though I were angry yesterday, with ye all,
And very angry for thought ye bobd me.

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab: No, no, by no meanes.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
No, when I considered
It was a jest, and carried off so quaintly
It made me merry: very merry, Gentlemen,
I doe confes I could not sleepe to thinke on’t
The mirth so tickled me, I could not slumber,

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
Good mirth do’s worke so: honest mirth,
Now, should we have meant in earnest—

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab: You say true Neighbour,

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
It might bred such a distant and sowrenes se,
Such fond imaginations in your Braines, Sir
For things trust home in earnest—

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
Very certaine
But I know ye all for merry waggs, and ere long
You shall know me too. in another fashion
Though y’are pamper’d ye shall beare part ߴoth burthen. Enter Amaranta and Leandro. Cross-hatched lines.
Come Wife; Come bid ’em wellcome; Come my Jewell:
And Pupill, you shall come too; nere hand backward,
Come, come the womans pleas’d, her angers over,
Come, be not bashfull,Algazers with dishes ready

sp.speaker: Am
sp.ab:
What do’s he prepare here?
Sure ther’s no meate ’ith house at least none drest,
Do’s he meane to mock ’em? or some new bred Crotchet
Come o’re his braines; I doe not like his kindnes?
But silence best becomes me: if he meane foule play
Sure they are enough to right themselves and let ’em,
I’ll sit by, so they beat him not to powder,

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab: (Neighbour

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
Bring in the meate there, ha? Sit downe deare
A little meate needs little Complement,
Sit downe I say:

sp.speaker: Am
sp.ab: What doe you meane by this Sir?

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab: Convay away their weapons handsomely,

sp.speaker: Am
sp.ab:
You know ther’s none ith’ house to answer ye,
But the poore Girle; you know ther’s no meat neither

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
Peace and be quiet; I shall make you smoak els
Ther’s men aud Meate enough, set it downe formally

sp.speaker: Am
sp.ab: I feare some lew’d tricke, yet I dare not speake on’t

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
I have no dainties for ye Gentlemen,
Nor lodes of meat, to make the roome smell of’em
Onely a dish to every man I have dedicated,
And if I have pleas’d his appetite,

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
O, a Capon,
A Bird of grace, and by thy will, I honour it

sp.speaker: Di
sp.ab:
For me some fortie pound of lovely Beeffe,
Plac’d in a mediterranean sea of Brewisse

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
Fall to fall to that we may drinke and laugh after
Wait diligently knaves,

sp.speaker: Mil
sp.ab:
What rare bits this?
An execution, bles se me!

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
Nay take it to ye
Ther’s no avoiding it ’tis somewhat tough Sir,
But a good stomach will endure it easely
The sum is, but a thousand duckets Sir,

sp.speaker: Ars
sp.ab: A Capias from my Surgeon, and my Silke man,

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
Your carefull makers but they have mard your diet
Stir not, your Swords are gon: ther’s no avoiding me
And these are Algazeirs, doe you heare that pas sing bell?

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab: A strong Citation, bles se me!

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
Out with your Beads, Curat
The devills in your dish: bell, booke, and Candell,

sp.speaker: Diego
sp.ab:
A warrant to appeare before the Judges?
I must needs rise, and turne to’th wall.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
Ye need not,
Your feare I hope will make ye find your Breeches,

sp.speaker: All
sp.ab: We are betraid

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
Invited, doe not wrong me,
Fall to, good Guests, you have dilligent men about ye,
Ye shall want nothing, that may persecute ye
These will not see ye start; Have I now found ye
Have I requited ye? You fool d the Lawyer,
And thought it meritorious, to abuse him,
A thick ram headed knave: you rid you spurd him,
And glorified your witts, the more ye wrongd him;
Within this hower, ye shall have all your Creditours,
A second dish of new debts, come upon ye
And new invitements to the whip (Don Diego)
And Excommunications for the Learned Curat,
A Masque of all your furies shall dance to ye,

sp.speaker: Ars
sp.ab: You dare not use us thus?

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
You shall be bobd (Gentlemen)
Stir, and as I have a life, ye goe to prison
To prison, without pittie instantly
Before ye speake another word to prison.
I have a better Guard, without, that waytes;
Doe you see this man, Don Curat? ’tis a Paratour
That comes to tell ye a delightfull story.
Of an old whore, ye have and then to teach ye
What is the penaltie; Laugh at me now Sir,
What Legacie would ye bequeath me now,
(And pay it on the naile?) to fly my fury?

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab: O gentle Sir,

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
Do’st thou hope I will be gentle,
Thou foolish unconsiderate Curat?

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab: Let me goe Sir,

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab: I’ll see thee hang first,

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab:
And as I am a true Vicar,
Hark in your eare hark softly—

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
No, no bribery.
I’ll have my swindge upon thee; Sirha? Rascall?
You lenten Chaps, you that lay sick, and mockt me,
Mockt me abhominably; abused me lewdly
I’ll make thee sick at heart, before I leave thee,
And groane, and dye indeed, and be worth nothing
Not worth a bles sing, nor a Bell to knell for thee,
A sheete to cover thee, but that thou stealest,
Stealest from the Merchant, and the Ring he was buried
with
Stealest from his Grave, doe you smell me now?

sp.speaker: Die
sp.ab: Have mercy on me!

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
No Psalme of mercy shall hold me from hanging
thee
How do ye like your Breakfast? ’tis but short, Gentlemen
But sweet and healthfull; Your punishment and your, Sir
For some neare reasons, that concerns my Credit,
I will take to my self.

sp.speaker: Am
sp.ab:
Doe Sir, and spare not
I have bin too good a wife, and too obedient,
But since ye dare provoke me to be foolish—

sp.speaker: Lea
sp.ab:
She has, yes, and too worthie of your usage,
Before the world, I justifie her goodnes,
And turne that man, that dares but taint her vertues,
To my Swords point; that lying man, that base man,
Turne him, but face to face, that I may know him

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab: What have I here?

sp.speaker: Lea
sp.ab:
A Gentleman, a free man,
One that made triall of this Ladies constancie,
And found it strong as fate; Leave off your fooling,
For it you follow this course, you will be Chronicled Enter Iamy and Assistant.
For a devill, whilst a Saint she is mentioned,
Yo know my name indeed; I am now no Lawyer.
Some comfort now, I hope, or els would I wer hanged up

sp.speaker: Die
sp.ab: And yet the Judge, he makes me swet.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab: What newes now?

sp.speaker: Iam
sp.ab:
I will justifie upon my life, and Credit
What you have heard, for truth, and will make prooffe of

sp.speaker: Assist
sp.ab:
I will be ready at the appointed hower there,
And so I leave ye.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
Stay I beseech your worship,
And doe but heare me,

sp.speaker: Iam
sp.ab:
Good Sir, intend this busines,
And let this bawling Foole; No more words Lawyer,
And no more angers for I gues se your reasons,
This Gentleman, i’l justifie in all places,
And that faire Ladies worth; Let who dare cros se it,
The Plot was cast by me, to make thee jealous,
But not to wrong your wife, she is faire and vertous,

sp.speaker: Die
sp.ab:
Take us to mercy too, we beseech your honour,
[...] shall be justified the way of all flesh els,
[...]. No more talke nor no more dissention Lawyer,
[...]w your anger, ’tis a vaine and slight one,
[...]ou doe; i’ll lay your whole life open
[...]hat all the world shall i’ll bring witnes,
[...]p before a Judge the ulcerous villanies
[...]know I know ye, and I can bring witnes.
[...]. Nay good Sir, noble Sir.

sp.speaker: [...m]
sp.ab:
Be at peace then presently,
[...]diately take honest and faire truce
[...] your good Wife and shake hands with that Gen
tleman;
[...]honour’d ye too much, and doe it cheerefully,

sp.speaker: Lop
sp.ab: Take us along, for heaven sake too.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
I am Friends,octa: Ja: ascanio be ready
[...]here is no remedie, I must put up all,
And like my neighbours rub it ou’t by’th shoulders;
And perfect friends; Leandro now I thanke ye,
And ther’s my hand, I have no more grudge to ye,
But I am too meane henceforward for your Companie,

sp.speaker: Lea
sp.ab: I shall not trouble ye,

sp.speaker: Ars
sp.ab: We will be friends too:

sp.speaker: Mil
sp.ab:
Nay Lawyer, you shall not fright us farther,
For all your devills wee will bolt,

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
I grant ye.
The Gentlemans your Baile, and thank him comming,
Did not he know me too well, you should smart for’t;
Goe all in peace, but when ye Foole next, Gentlemen,
Come not to me to Breakefast.

sp.speaker: Die
sp.ab: I’l be bak’d first.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
And pray ye remember, when ye are bold & merry,
The Lawyers Bancket, and the Sawce he gave ye,

sp.speaker: Iam
sp.ab:
Come: goe along; I have employment for ye,
Employment for your lewd braynes too, to coole ye.
For all, for every one.

sp.speaker: All
sp.ab: We are all your Servants.

sp.speaker: Die
sp.ab:
All, all for any thing, from this day forward,
I’l hate all Breakefasts, and depend on dinners

sp.speaker: Iam
sp.ab: I am glad you come off faire

sp.speaker: Lea
sp.ab: The faire has blest me.

sp.speaker: Oct
sp.ab:
This is the place, but why are appointed
By Don Jami to stay here, is a depthHenry & Jami be ready
I cannot sound,

sp.speaker: Asc
sp.ab:
Beleev’t he is too noble,
To purpose any thing but for our good
Had I as surance of a thousand Lives,
And with them perpetuitie of pleasures,
And should loose all, if he prov’d only false,
Yet I durst run the hazard,

sp.speaker: Iac
sp.ab:
’Tis our comfort,
We cannot be more wretched then we are,
And death concludes all misery,

sp.speaker: Oct
sp.ab:
Undiscovered Enter Henrique, Iami. Cross-hatched lines.
We must attend him

sp.speaker: Asc
sp.ab:
Our stay is not long
With him Don Henrique?

sp.speaker: Iac
sp.ab:
Now I feare;
Be silent.

sp.speaker: Hen
sp.ab: Why do’st thou follow me?

sp.speaker: Iam
sp.ab:
To save your life,
A plot is laid for’t, all my wrongs forgot,
I have a Brothers Love.Le: Mill: ar: bar be ready

sp.speaker: Hen
sp.ab:
But thy false self,
I feare no enemy.

sp.speaker: Iam
sp.ab:
You have no Friend,
But what breathes in me: If you move a step
Beyond this ground you tread on: you are lost.

sp.speaker: Hen
sp.ab:
’Tis by thy practice then: I am sent hither
To meete her, that prefers my life, and safetie
Before her owne.

sp.speaker: Iam
sp.ab:
That you should be abus’d’thus
With weake credulitie: She for whose sake,
You have forgot we had one noble Father,
Or that one Mother bare us, for whose love,
You breake a contract, to which heaven was witnes,
To satisfie whose pride, and willfull humour,
You have expos’d a sweet, and hopefull Son,
To all the miseries, that want can bring him,
And such a Son, though you are the most obdurate,
To give whom entertainement Savages
Would quit their Caves themselves, to keepe him from
Bleake cold, and hunger: This dis sembling Woman,
This Idoll, whom you worship: all your love
And service trod under her feete, designes you
To fill a grave or dead to lye a pray,
For Wolves, and vultures.

sp.speaker: Hen
sp.ab:
’Tis false; I defie thee,
And stand upon my GuardCross-hatched lines.

div.stage: Enter Leandro Millanes, Arsenio, Bart. Lopez, Diego, Octavio Iacinta Ascanio and Servants.

sp.speaker: Iam
sp.ab:
Alas, ’tis weake:
Come on since you will teach me to be cruell,
By having no faith, in me, take your fortune,
Bring the rest forth, and bind them fast.

sp.speaker: Oct
sp.ab: My Lord.

sp.speaker: Asc
sp.ab: In what have we offended?

sp.speaker: Iam
sp.ab:
I am deafe,
And following my will, I doe not standViolante be ready
Accomptable to reason: See her Ring
(The first pledge of your love, and service to her)
Delivered as a Warrant for your death:
These Bags of gold you gave up to her trust,
(The use of which, you did deny your selfe)
Bestow’d on me, and with a prodigal! hand,
Whom she pick’d forth to be the Architect
Of her most bloudy building; and to See
These Instruments, to bring Materials
To raise it up, she bad me spare no cost,
And (as a surplusage) offer’d her selfe
To be at my devotion.

sp.speaker: Henr
sp.ab: O accurss’d!

sp.speaker: Iam
sp.ab:
But be incredulous still; think this my plot;
Fashion excuses to your selfe, and sweare
That she is innocent, that she doats on ye;
Believe this, as a fearefull Dreame, and that
You lie not at my mercy, which in this
I will shew onely: She her selfe shall give
The dreadfull Sentence, to remove all scruple
Who ’tis that sends you to the other world. Enter Violante. Cross-hatched lines. assistant 7amp: officers be ready
Appeares my Violante? speake (my dearest)
Do’s not the object please you?

sp.speaker: Viol
sp.ab:
More then if
All Treasure that’s above the earth, with that,
That lyes conceal’d in both the Indian Mines,
Were laid downe at my feet: O bold Iamy
Thou onely canst deserve me.

sp.speaker: Iam,
sp.ab:
I am forward,
And (as you easily may perceive,) I sleepe not
On your commands.

sp.speaker: Viol
sp.ab:
But yet they live: I look’d
To find them dead.

sp.speaker: Iam
sp.ab:
That was defer’d, that you
Might triumph in their misery, and have the powre
To say they are not,

sp.speaker: Viol
sp.ab:
’Twas well thought upon:
This kis se, and all the pleasures of my Bed
This night, shall thank thee.

sp.speaker: Hen
sp.ab: Monster!

sp.speaker: Viol
sp.ab:
You Sir, that
Would have me mother Bastards, being unable
To honour me with one Child of mine owne,
That underneath my Roofe, kept your cast-Strumpet,
And out of my Revenues, would maintaine
Her riotous is sue: Now you find what ’tis
To tempt a woman: with as little feeling
As I turne off a slave, that is unfit
To doe me service; of a horse, or dog
That have out-liv’d their use, I shake thee off,
To make thy peace with heaven.

sp.speaker: Hen
sp.ab:
I doe deserve this,
And never truly felt before, what sorrow
Attends on willfull dotage.

sp.speaker: Viol
sp.ab:
For you, Misstris,
That had the pleasure of his youth before me,
And triumph’d in the fruit, that you had by him,
But that I thinke, to have the Bastard strangled
Before thy face, and thou with speed to follow
The way he leades thee, is sufficent torture,
I would cut off thy nose, put out thine eyes,
And set my foot on these bewitching lips,
That had the start of mine: but as thou art,
Goe to the grave unpittied.

sp.speaker: Assist
sp.ab:
Who would beleeve
Such rage could be in woman?

sp.speaker: Viol,
sp.ab:
For this Fellow,
He is not worth my knowledge.

sp.speaker: Iam
sp.ab:
Let him live then,
Since you esteeme him innocent.

sp.speaker: Viol
sp.ab:
No, Jamy,
He shall make up the mes se: now strike together
And let them fall so.

sp.speaker: Assist
sp.ab:
Unheard of crueltie!
I can endure no longer: seize on her.

sp.speaker: Viol
sp.ab:
Am I betrai’d?
Is this thy faith, Iamy?

sp.speaker: Iam
sp.ab:
Could your desires
Challenge performance of a deed so horrid?
Or, though that you had sold your selfe to hell,
I should make up the bargaine? Live (deare Brother)
Live long, and happy: I forgive you freely;
To have done you this serviee, is to me
A faire Inheritance: And how e’re harsh language
(Call’d on, by your rough usage) pass’d my lipps,
In my heart, I ever lov’d you: All my labours
Were but to shew, how much your love was cozen’d,
When it beheld it selfe in this false Glas se,
That did abuse you; and I am so far
From envying young Ascanio his good fortune,
That if your State were mine, I would adopt him.
These are the Murtherers, my noble Friends,
Which (to make triall of her bloudy purpose)
I won, to come disguis’d thus.

sp.speaker: Hen
sp.ab:
I am too full
Of griefe, and shame to speake: but what I’le doe,
Shall to the world proclaime my penitence;
And howsoever I have liv’d, I’le die
A much chang’d man.

sp.speaker: Iam
sp.ab:
Were it but pos sible
You could make satisfaction to this woman,
Our joyes were perfect.

sp.speaker: Hen
sp.ab:
That’s my onely comfort,
That it is in my power: I ne’re was married
To this bad woman, though I doted on her,
But daily did deferre it, still expecting
When griefe would kill Jacintha.

sp.speaker: Assist
sp.ab:
All is come out,
And finds a faire succes se: take her Don Henrique,
And once againe embrace your Son.

sp.speaker: Hen
sp.ab: Most gladly.

sp.speaker: Assist
sp.ab: Your Brother hath deserv’d well.

sp.speaker: Hen
sp.ab:
And shall share
The moitie of my State,

sp.speaker: Assist
sp.ab:
I have heart, Advocate,
What an ill Instrument you have bin to him,
For this time strengthen him, with honest counsells,
As you’le deserve my pardon.

sp.speaker: Bar
sp.ab:
I’le change my Copy:
But I am punish’d, for I feare I have had
A smart blow, though unseene.

sp.speaker: Assist
sp.ab:
Curat, and Sexton,
I have heard of you too, let me heare no more,
And what’s past, is forgotten; For this woman,
Though her intent were bloody, yet our Law
Calls it not death: yet that her punishment May
50
May deter others from such bad attempts,
The Dowry she brought with her shall be emploi’d
To build a Nunnery, where she shall spend
The remnant of her life.

sp.speaker: Viol
sp.ab:
Since I have miss’d my ends,
I scorne what can fall on me.

sp.speaker: Assist
sp.ab:
The strict discipline
Of the Church, will teach you better thoughts. and Sig
niors,-
You that are Batchelours, if you ever marry,
In Bartolus, you may behold the is sue
Of Covetousnesse, and Jealousie; And of dotage,
and falshood in, Don Henrique, keep a meane then;
For be as sur’d that weake man meets all ill,
That gives himselfe up to a womans will.

div.label: Epilogue.
div.sp:
THe Play is done, yet our suit never ends,
Still when you part, you would stil part our friends,
Our noblest friends; if ought have falne amis,
O let it be sufficient, that it is,
And you have pardon’d it. In Buildings great
All the whole Body, cannot be so neat,
But something may be mended; Those are faire,
And worthy love, that may destroy, but spare.
